title: Deep SiMLR: Auditable Multi-Modal Integration for Biomedical Discovery
text:
Abstract
Multi-modal biomedical datasets—such as co-registered neuroimaging, high-throughput omics, and clinical assessments—provide complementary views of shared pathological processes. Integrating these heterogeneous matrices requires dimensionality reduction that isolates cross-view covariance while maintaining interpretable feature attribution. Standard deep multi-view networks and variational autoencoders capture non-linear interactions, but their nested compositions obscure the physical relationship between raw biological measurements and latent coordinates, imposing a severe “transparency penalty” that precludes regulatory adoption in high-stakes clinical decision-making. Conversely, classical linear methods like Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) provide auditable projections, but fail to capture non-linear manifold geometry and produce dense, mixed-sign loadings that lack anatomical specificity.
To eliminate this transparency penalty without sacrificing representation capacity, we formulate Deep SiMLR (Similarity-driven Multi-view Reconstruction) governed by the Only Linear Encoder Entrypoint (OLEE) contract. OLEE mandates that the initial entrypoint for every modality is restricted to a linear projection on the compact Stiefel manifold (\(\mathbf{Z}_m = \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m\), subject to \(\mathbf{V}_m^\top \mathbf{V}_m = \mathbf{I}_k\)). This structural contract guarantees globally constant attribution derivatives (\(\nabla_{\mathbf{X}_m} \mathbf{Z}_m = \mathbf{V}_m\)) and enables closed-form counterfactual auditability (\(\Delta \mathbf{Z}_m = \Delta \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m\) and \(\delta \mathbf{x}_m^* = \Delta \mathbf{z}_m \mathbf{V}_m^\top\)), connecting mathematical dimensionality reduction directly to causal recourse principles. Downstream transformations—including volume-preserving normalizing flows (Flow-SiMR-V), bound-constrained quasi-Newton Riemannian solvers (SiMLR-LBFGSB, SiMLR-LBFGS), and non-linear decoders (LEND)—model non-linear geometry while preserving exact first-order input auditability. Spectral Modality Alignment Index (MAI) dynamic weighting down-weights uninformative modalities, preventing isotropic noise from corrupting consensus discovery.
We benchmark nine architectures across 243 task evaluations spanning nine multi-modal data regimes (six synthetic manifolds with known ground truth and three public clinical/multi-omics cohorts: UCI Cleveland Heart Disease, Efron Diabetes Progression, and 3-assay TCGA-BRCA multi-omics) across three independent seeds (private_scale = 0.5, consolidate = False, default "pca" initialization), alongside a dedicated 4-view study of Mild Cognitive Impairment in the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI-MCI, \(N=1,084\)). Following Demšar’s block-level ranking protocol across the nine datasets, non-parametric inference confirms significant architectural separation (Friedman \(\chi_F^2 = 32.47, p = 7.68 \times 10^{-5}\); Iman–Davenport \(F_F = 6.57, p = 3.13 \times 10^{-6}\); Nemenyi Critical Difference \(CD = 4.004\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\)). Across global consensus predictions, bound-constrained quasi-Newton SiMLR-LBFGSB achieves the top overall rank (mean rank \(3.28\), predictive score \(0.795 \pm 0.201\), support recovery \(0.942\)), closely followed by hybrid LEND (mean rank \(3.56\), highest mean predictive score \(0.830 \pm 0.189\), highest linear probe \(0.836\), highest axis-sensitive probe \(0.830\), and highest ground-truth latent recovery \(CMC = 0.907\)), single-matrix NSAFlow-PCA (mean rank \(3.61\), \(0.782 \pm 0.200\) in \(0.029\text{s}\), leading Diabetes \(R^2 = 0.382\), Heart accuracy \(83.7\%\), and TCGA-BRCA accuracy \(92.7\%\)), and PCA (mean rank \(3.78\), \(0.774 \pm 0.213\) in \(0.024\text{s}\), \(0.0\%\) sparsity, chance support recovery \(0.333\)). On regimes with asymmetric view-private variance (Shared+Private) or weak sparse parts (NonnegPartsWeak), cross-view OLEE consensus (LEND \(R^2 = 0.949\) and \(0.732\); SiMLR-LBFGSB \(R^2 = 0.715\)) substantially outperforms single-matrix concatenation (PCA \(R^2 = 0.639\) and \(0.522\)). In ADNI-MCI (\(N=1,084\)), we show in plain clinical terms why predicting daily functional disability (Clinical Dementia Rating Sum of Boxes, CDR-SB) directly from 382 structural brain MRI features explains only \(4.1\%\) of test-set variance (\(R^2 = 0.0411\)): brain tissue loss does not directly cause difficulties with daily chores, but instead first impairs cognitive abilities (memory and executive function), which in turn drive daily disability. Modeling this two-step pathway by aligning three brain MRI views (\(382\) features) with a 13-item cognitive test view increases out-of-sample CDR-SB prediction over six-fold (\(R^2 = 0.2648\) for LEND-SiMR + MAI; \(R^2 = 0.2443\) in \(0.86\text{s}\) for SiMLR), with \(85\text{–}86\%\) of the brain-structure effect acting indirectly through cognition (\(p < 10^{-15}\)). On this cohort, unconstrained deep encoders without a linear first layer overfit the 382 MRI features and collapse on held-out patients (NED-SiMR \(R^2 = 0.1127\)), demonstrating that the OLEE linear entrypoint provides an essential safeguard against high-dimensional overfitting while preserving direct biomarker auditability.

title: 1  Introduction and Background
text:
1.1 Introduction
High-throughput biomedical studies routinely collect multiple distinct measurements from each subject. In neurodegenerative disease research, cohorts such as the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) (Weiner et al. 2017; Jack et al. 2008) and the Parkinson’s Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) (Marek et al. 2011) acquire structural MRI regional morphometry, diffusion tensor white matter fractional anisotropy, molecular PET, biofluid assays, and comprehensive psychometric batteries (Avants et al. 2014; Stone et al. 2020; Avants et al. 2021). In traumatic brain injury (TBI) and neurotrauma, blast-induced shockwave exposure produces diffuse axonal injury and non-local microstructural shearing that alter structural connectivity networks (Stone et al. 2024). In translational oncology, the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) profiles patient tumors across somatic copy-number alterations, transcriptomic expression, DNA methylation, and targeted reverse-phase protein arrays in breast invasive carcinoma (BRCA) (The Cancer Genome Atlas Network 2012; Cancer Discovery 2016) and clear cell renal cell carcinoma (KIRC) (The Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network 2013). Integrating these observations—formalized as \(M\) data matrices \(\mathbf{X}_m \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p_m}\) for \(m = 1, \dots, M\) across \(n\) co-registered subjects—is essential for resolving phenotypic heterogeneity, identifying molecular subtypes, and mapping progression trajectories.
Deep representation learning methods, including Deep Canonical Correlation Analysis (Deep CCA) (Andrew et al. 2013) and Multimodal Variational Autoencoders (MVAEs) (Wu and Goodman 2018), capture non-linear cross-modal dependencies. However, standard deep encoders map inputs through deeply nested affine transformations interleaved with non-linear activations (\(\mathbf{Z} = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_2 \sigma(\mathbf{W}_1 \mathbf{X} + \mathbf{b}_1) + \mathbf{b}_2)\)). This composition creates complex feature entanglement, obscuring the physical attribution between observable biological measurements and latent coordinates (Rudin 2019). In clinical diagnostics, oncology biomarker discovery, and neurotrauma assessment, this opacity imposes a severe transparency penalty: clinicians, regulatory agencies, and trial biostatisticians cannot determine whether a diagnostic score reflects authentic pathophysiology (such as entorhinal cortical atrophy or targeted kinase dysregulation) or idiosyncratic scanner noise and batch artifacts (Holmberg et al. 2022).
Post-hoc explainability techniques, such as LIME (Ribeiro et al. 2016) and SHAP (Lundberg and Lee 2017), attempt to infer feature importance by querying black-box models on randomly perturbed inputs. As demonstrated by Rudin (2019), post-hoc surrogates exhibit fundamental failure modes in biological domains. By perturbing features independently, they evaluate synthetic samples that violate physiological covariance—pairing, for example, incompatible regional brain volumes or mutually exclusive oncogenic mutations. Consequently, post-hoc explanations can be unstable, sensitive to hyperparameter tuning, and biologically deceptive (Radulovic 2023).
Conversely, classical linear dimensionality reduction methods—including Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) (Hotelling 1936)—provide exact linear loadings (\(Z_{jk} = \sum_i X_{ji} V_{ik}\)). Similarity-driven Multimodal Linear Reconstruction (SiMLR) (Avants et al. 2021) extended CCA to multiple modalities with sparsity and non-negativity constraints, solving a joint-variational problem on the Stiefel manifold. While linear SiMLR guarantees interpretability, complex disease processes can involve non-linear manifold geometry that linear projections cannot span. Furthermore, unconstrained PCA yields dense, mixed-sign loadings that lack anatomical specificity and fail to isolate shared cross-modal signals from modality-specific noise.

title: 1  Introduction and Background
text:
1.1.1 The Only Linear Encoder Entrypoint (OLEE) Contract
To resolve the tension between non-linear expressivity and auditable feature attribution, we formulate Deep SiMLR governed by the Only Linear Encoder Entrypoint (OLEE) contract. OLEE mandates that the initial entrypoint for every modality is restricted to a linear projection on the compact Stiefel manifold: \[
\mathbf{Z}_m = \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m, \quad \text{subject to } \mathbf{V}_m \in \text{St}(k, p_m) = \{\mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{p_m \times k} \mid \mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{V} = \mathbf{I}_k\}
\] All downstream non-linear transformations—including volume-preserving normalizing flows, Riemannian quasi-Newton solvers, and non-linear decoders—operate exclusively on the low-dimensional latent coordinates \(\mathbf{Z}_m \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}\).
Enforcing the OLEE contract yields three fundamental mathematical and clinical guarantees:

Elimination of the Transparency Penalty: Because the input mapping is strictly linear, the directional attribution gradient with respect to raw physical features is globally constant and analytically exact: \[
\nabla_{\mathbf{X}_m} \mathbf{Z}_m = \mathbf{V}_m, \quad \frac{\partial Z_{m, ik}}{\partial X_{m, ij}} = V_{m, jk}
\] Unlike black-box encoders where local gradients vary wildly across the input manifold, the OLEE loading matrix \(\mathbf{V}_m\) directly encodes the physical contribution of every biological feature.
Closed-Form Counterfactual Recourse: In causal recourse and actionable intervention frameworks (Pearl 2009; Wachter et al. 2017), a critical objective is determining what observable biomarker intervention \(\Delta \mathbf{x}\) will produce a desired therapeutic shift \(\Delta \mathbf{z}^*\) in disease state. Under standard deep encoders, calculating recourse requires non-convex gradient descent through non-linear latents, regularly synthesizing physically impossible biological states. Under the OLEE contract, forward latent shifts are instantaneous: \[
\Delta \mathbf{Z}_m = \Delta \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m
\] while the minimal \(L_2\)-norm physical intervention required to achieve a target shift \(\Delta \mathbf{z}_m^*\) is an exact orthogonal projection: \[
\delta \mathbf{x}_m^* = \Delta \mathbf{z}_m^* \mathbf{V}_m^\top
\] This delivers immediate, closed-form causal auditability without heuristic sampling.
Spectral Noise Insulation: To prevent high-dimensional isotropic noise from distorting consensus coordinates, we incorporate dynamic Modality Alignment Index (MAI) weighting based on singular value decay, down-weighting uninformative modalities during consensus optimization.



1.1.2 Multimodal Consensus as Latent Signal Recovery
We formalize multi-view integration as the estimation of a shared latent signal \(\mathbf{S} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}\) from \(M\) observations: \[
\mathbf{X}_m = g_m(\mathbf{S}) + \mathbf{E}_m, \quad m = 1, \dots, M
\] where \(g_m: \mathbb{R}^{n \times k} \to \mathbb{R}^{n \times p_m}\) is a modality-specific generative mapping and \(\mathbf{E}_m\) represents domain-specific noise and private variance. Multi-modal consensus seeks mappings \(f_m(\mathbf{X}_m)\) that project each observation to a unified consensus representation \(\mathbf{U} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}\) approximating \(\mathbf{S}\).
In biological cohorts, ambient feature dimensions often far exceed sample size (\(p_m \gg n\)). When a high-dimensional view contains little structured covariance, standard correlation objectives can capitalize on chance associations, corrupting the consensus space (Avants et al. 2025; Stone et al. 2024). Principled integration requires explicit regularization that penalizes off-manifold noise while preserving true biological signal.


1.1.3 Why Brain MRI Needs Cognitive Mediation to Predict Daily Disability in ADNI-MCI
A clear real-world example of why multi-view alignment and a linear first layer (OLEE) matter comes from predicting daily functional decline in \(N = 1,084\) patients with Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) in the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) (Weiner et al. 2017; Jack et al. 2008). In clinical trials, the standard outcome used to judge whether a treatment works is the Clinical Dementia Rating – Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB), a clinical score measuring how much difficulty a patient has with everyday tasks such as managing money, remembering appointments, shopping, and personal care.
Each patient has four views of baseline data (after adjusting for age, sex, and years of education):

Three structural brain MRI views (\(382\) brain regions total): regional gray-matter volumes (\(p_1 = 160\)), hierarchical cortical surface thickness (\(p_2 = 160\)), and native T1-weighted cortical thickness (\(p_3 = 62\)).
One cognitive test view (\(p_4 = 13\) items): bedside memory, language, and executive-function sub-scores from the ADAS-Cog and MMSE batteries.

Comparing different ways of predicting CDR-SB on held-out patients reveals three simple findings:

Predicting daily disability directly from brain MRI barely works (\(R^2 = 0.0411\)): When a model tries to predict CDR-SB directly from the 382 brain MRI measurements alone, it explains only \(4.1\%\) of the variance on unseen test patients (\(\text{Direct-Anatomy [SiMLR]}: R^2 = 0.0411 \pm 0.0248, \rho = 0.2203\)), and standard ridge regression on the concatenated MRI features fails completely (\(R^2 = -0.1810 \pm 0.0916\)). The reason is simple biology: tissue loss in the hippocampus or temporal cortex does not directly make a person unable to balance a checkbook. Instead, brain atrophy first impairs cognitive test performance (memory and thinking), and that cognitive decline is what causes trouble with daily activities.
Modeling the two-step pathway (\(\text{Brain MRI} \to \text{Shared Cognitive Summary} \to \text{CDR-SB}\)) boosts prediction 6-fold (\(R^2 = 0.2648\)): When we align the three brain MRI views (\(382\) features) with the 13 cognitive test items to learn a shared cognitive-anatomical summary (\(Z_{\text{cog}}\)) and use that summary to predict CDR-SB, out-of-sample accuracy jumps more than six-fold:

\(\text{LEND-SiMR + MAI [Mediated]}\): \(R^2 = 0.2648 \pm 0.0332\) (\(6.44\times\) higher than direct MRI, \(\rho = 0.5206\), paired Wilcoxon \(p = 9.77 \times 10^{-4}\) vs. covariates).
\(\text{SiMLR [Mediated]}\): \(R^2 = 0.2443 \pm 0.0534\) (\(5.94\times\) higher than direct MRI, \(\rho = 0.4989\)) in just \(0.86\text{ seconds}\).
\(\text{Flow-SiMR-V + MAI [Mediated]}\): \(R^2 = 0.2290 \pm 0.0696\) (\(5.57\times\) higher than direct MRI).

Baron–Kenny and bootstrap mediation testing confirm that \(84.5\%\text{–}86.4\%\) of the effect of brain MRI atrophy on daily disability is indirect, acting through cognitive performance (\(p < 10^{-15}\)).
Unconstrained deep encoders overfit the 382 MRI features and collapse on test patients (\(R^2 = 0.1127\)): When we replace the linear Stiefel entrypoint with an unconstrained multi-layer perceptron encoder on the same two-step pathway, test-set performance drops by more than half (\(\text{NED-SiMR + MAI [Mediated]}: R^2 = 0.1127 \pm 0.0578\); \(\text{NED-Shared-Private}: R^2 = 0.0840 \pm 0.0412\)). With \(382\) correlated MRI measurements and roughly \(750\) training patients per fold, a flexible deep encoder memorizes noisy training-set correlations. Restricting the first layer to an orthonormal linear projection (\(\mathbf{V}_m^\top \mathbf{V}_m = \mathbf{I}_k\)) acts as a strong geometric safeguard against overfitting while keeping every brain region’s weight directly readable.

1.2 Background

1.2.1 Subspace Invariance versus Basis Axis Sensitivity
When evaluating multi-view representations, it is essential to distinguish between the subspace spanned by a projection and the individual coordinate axes:

Subspace Invariance: For any orthogonal transformation \(\mathbf{M} \in O(k)\), the rotated representation \(\mathbf{Z}_m \mathbf{M} = \mathbf{X}_m (\mathbf{V}_m \mathbf{M})\) spans the identical linear subspace as \(\mathbf{Z}_m\). Linear models trained on \(\mathbf{Z}_m \mathbf{M}\) achieve identical predictions to those trained on \(\mathbf{Z}_m\).
Axis Sensitivity: Identifying individual anatomical or molecular biomarkers requires that specific coordinate axes align with meaningful physical factors. Axis-sensitive probes, such as axis-aligned decision trees and random forests, depend on the specific orientation of \(\mathbf{V}_m\).
Signed Support Disjointness: In non-negative or contrast-split representations (\(\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{V}^+ - \mathbf{V}^-\) with \(\mathbf{V}^+, \mathbf{V}^- \ge 0\)), overlap between positive and negative lobes produces destructive cancellation. Enforcing disjoint support (\(\mathbf{V}^+ \odot \mathbf{V}^- = \mathbf{0}\)) eliminates crosstalk, ensuring that positive and negative coefficients index distinct feature sets.

Figure 1.1: Architectural Comparison of the Interpretability Gap. Unconstrained deep multi-view encoders entangle input features across hidden layers, requiring post-hoc perturbation surrogates (SHAP/LIME). The Stiefel-constrained Only Linear Encoder Entrypoint (OLEE) enforces an orthonormal linear basis \(\mathbf{V}_m\) (\(\mathbf{V}_m^\top \mathbf{V}_m = \mathbf{I}_k\)) at the input boundary, guaranteeing exact constant attribution (\(\nabla_{\mathbf{X}_m}\mathbf{Z}_m = \mathbf{V}_m\)) and closed-form counterfactual recourse (\(\delta \mathbf{x}_m^* = \Delta \mathbf{z}_m \mathbf{V}_m^\top\)) prior to downstream non-linear decoding or normalizing flows.





1.2.2 Architectural Taxonomy
We evaluate nine distinct architectures spanning linear baselines, manifold-regularized linear solvers, hybrid autoencoders, and normalizing flows:

PCA (Classical Linear Baseline): Standard Principal Component Analysis fitted via singular value decomposition on concatenated, standardized features (\(\mathbf{X} = [\mathbf{X}_1 \dots \mathbf{X}_M]\)). Establishes the unconstrained dense linear baseline.
NSAFlow-PCA (Accelerated Non-negative Stiefel Flow): A fast single-matrix manifold solver utilizing direct SVD initialization on concatenated features and differentiable Non-negative Stiefel Approximating Flow (nsa_flow) retraction in \(0.029\text{s}\).
SiMLR (Riemannian Gradient Descent): The classical linear cross-view formulation solving the multi-view alignment problem via Armijo line-search gradient descent with per-sweep NSA-Flow retraction.
SiMLR-LBFGS (Quasi-Newton Riemannian): A linear cross-view architecture incorporating two-loop L-BFGS curvature steps on the Stiefel manifold with per-sweep NSA-Flow retraction.
SiMLR-LBFGSB (Bound-Constrained Quasi-Newton): A linear cross-view architecture using the NSA-Flow bound-constrained L-BFGS-B solver (nsa_lbfgsb), enforcing \(\mathbf{V}_m \ge \mathbf{0}\) inside the quasi-Newton step itself when positivity is active.
LEND (Linear Encoder, Non-linear Decoder): A hybrid OLEE architecture coupling per-view linear Stiefel projections (\(\mathbf{Z}_m = \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m\)) with a multi-layer perceptron decoder for non-linear feature reconstruction and cross-view consensus alignment.
Flow-SiMR-V (Bijective Normalizing Flow with Stiefel Bottleneck): An invertible OLEE architecture prepending a linear Stiefel projection matrix to volume-preserving RealNVP affine coupling layers in \(\mathbb{R}^k\), enabling continuous density estimation, exact invertibility, and conditional cross-view imputation.
NED (Non-linear Encoder-Decoder): A deep architecture adding hidden non-linear encoder layers after the initial linear projection.
NEDPP (Shared and Private Subspaces): An extension of NED that partitions latent coordinates into shared consensus and view-specific private subspaces using cross-covariance penalties.



1.2.3 Summary of Contributions

The Only Linear Encoder Entrypoint (OLEE) Contract: We formalize how restricting the input layer of multi-view encoders to the compact Stiefel manifold eliminates the clinical transparency penalty (\(\nabla_{\mathbf{X}_m} \mathbf{Z}_m = \mathbf{V}_m\)) and enables closed-form counterfactual recourse (\(\delta \mathbf{x}_m^* = \Delta \mathbf{z}_m^* \mathbf{V}_m^\top\), connecting directly to Pearl (2009) and Wachter et al. (2017)) while preserving downstream non-linear capacity.
Cognitive Mediation vs. Direct Brain MRI in ADNI-MCI: We explain and quantify why predicting daily disability (CDR-SB) directly from 382 brain MRI features hits a low ceiling (\(R^2 = 0.0411\)), demonstrate how aligning brain MRI with cognitive tests in a two-step pathway boosts out-of-sample accuracy over 6-fold (\(R^2 = 0.2648\) for LEND-SiMR + MAI; \(R^2 = 0.2443\) in \(0.86\text{s}\) for SiMLR; \(85\text{–}86\%\) indirect effect, \(p < 10^{-15}\)), and show how the OLEE linear first layer prevents the severe test-set overfitting seen in unconstrained deep encoders (NED-SiMR \(R^2 = 0.1127\)).
Bound-Constrained Quasi-Newton Manifold Optimization (SiMLR-LBFGSB, SiMLR-LBFGS): We show that coupling L-BFGS-B / L-BFGS optimization with NSA-Flow retractions achieves the top global Friedman rank (\(3.28\) for SiMLR-LBFGSB) and the highest sparse ground-truth support recovery (\(0.942\) vs. PCA \(0.333\)).
Hybrid Linear-Encoder Deep Decoding (LEND): We demonstrate that pairing an auditable linear encoder with a non-linear MLP decoder achieves the highest mean predictive performance (\(0.830 \pm 0.189\)), the highest ground-truth latent recovery (\(CMC = 0.907\)), and a decisive advantage when views carry strong view-private noise (Shared+Private: \(R^2 = 0.949\) vs. PCA \(0.639\)) or when outcomes lie in weak sparse components (NonnegPartsWeak: \(R^2 = 0.732\) vs. PCA \(0.522\)).
Rigorous Non-Parametric Demšar Benchmark: Across 243 task evaluations (9 data regimes—6 synthetic manifolds and 3 real clinical/multi-omics cohorts—\(\times\) 3 independent seeds \(\times\) 9 models), we conduct block-level Friedman (\(\chi_F^2 = 32.47, p = 7.68 \times 10^{-5}\)), Iman–Davenport (\(F_F = 6.57, p = 3.13 \times 10^{-6}\)), and Wilcoxon–Holm tests.
Multi-Objective 4-Axis Pareto Characterization: We map the empirical Pareto frontier across predictive accuracy (\(Y\)), ground-truth latent and support discovery (\(CMC\), Jaccard support), mathematical invariants (\(D\), zero crosstalk), and execution latency (\(t\)), identifying the operational trade-offs governing clinical deployment.

text: 2.1 Theoretical Foundation

title: 2  Methods
text:
2.1.1 The Multi-Modal Inverse Problem
We frame multi-modal representation learning as a structured inverse problem over \(M\) distinct observational domains. Let \(\mathbf{X}_m \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p_m}\) denote the centered observation matrix for modality \(m \in \{1, \dots, M\}\), where \(n\) is the number of co-registered subjects and \(p_m\) is the ambient feature dimensionality. Each modality provides a partial, noisy observation of an underlying shared latent biological state \(\mathbf{S} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}\) governed by modality-specific forward generative processes: \[
\mathbf{X}_m = g_m(\mathbf{S}) + \mathbf{E}_m
\tag{2.1}\] where \(g_m: \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^{p_m}\) is a smooth generative map applied row-wise across observations, and \(\mathbf{E}_m\) represents domain-specific observational noise and idiosyncratic variance. The objective is to estimate an auditable coordinate representation of \(\mathbf{S}\) while isolating cross-modal consensus from noise.


2.1.2 OLEE as a Structural Information Bottleneck
Standard deep autoencoders and multi-layer perceptrons process inputs via unconstrained mappings \(\mathbf{Z} = \text{MLP}(\mathbf{X})\). Following Tishby’s Information Bottleneck principle (Tishby et al. 2000), deep networks entangle mutual information across successive layers, readily memorizing high-dimensional noise and structured nuisance variables. In biomedical discovery, this produces severe latent collapse and obscures physical feature attribution.
We resolve this entanglement by enforcing the Only Linear Encoder Entrypoint (OLEE). OLEE mandates that the initial transformation of any modality \(\mathbf{X}_m\) is an orthogonal linear projection onto the compact Stiefel manifold \(\text{St}(k, p_m) = \{ \mathbf{V}_m \in \mathbb{R}^{p_m \times k} \mid \mathbf{V}_m^\top \mathbf{V}_m = \mathbf{I}_k \}\) (Edelman et al. 1998; Boumal 2023): \[
\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}} = \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}
\tag{2.2}\] Because the intrinsic dimension is strictly bounded (\(k \ll p_m\)) and \(\mathbf{V}_m\) acts as a partial isometry, OLEE imposes a structural information bottleneck at the input layer. All subsequent non-linear operations (decoders, prediction heads, or normalizing flows) consume \(\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}}\), never raw features \(\mathbf{X}_m\). This guarantees that downstream transformations operate on an auditable coordinate system with closed-form directional derivatives \(\nabla_{\mathbf{X}_m} \mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}} = \mathbf{V}_m\).


2.1.3 Joint-Variational Optimization Framework
We unify the Similarity-driven Multimodal Linear Representation (SiMLR) taxonomy under a joint-variational functional. For each modality \(m \in \{1, \dots, M\}\), we optimize an encoder \(f_m: \mathbb{R}^{p_m} \to \mathbb{R}^k\) and a decoder \(g_m: \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^{p_m}\), yielding latent representations \(\mathbf{Z}_m = f_m(\mathbf{X}_m) \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}\) and reconstructions \(\hat{\mathbf{X}}_m = g_m(\mathbf{Z}_m)\). The global variational functional balances within-modality reconstruction fidelity, cross-modal consensus alignment, and Stiefel manifold regularization:
\[
\min_{\{f_m, g_m\}_{m=1}^M} \sum_{m=1}^M \left[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{recon}}(\mathbf{X}_m, g_m(\mathbf{Z}_m)) + \lambda_{\text{sim}} \mathcal{L}_{\text{align}}(\mathbf{Z}_m, \mathbf{U}_{\neq m}) + \gamma D(\mathbf{V}_m) \right] + \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{Z})
\tag{2.3}\]
where:

\(\mathbf{U}_{\neq m} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}\) is the Leave-One-Out (LOO) consensus target derived from all modalities excluding modality \(m\): \[
\mathbf{U}_{\neq m} = \text{Consensus}\left( \{\mathbf{Z}_j\}_{j \neq m} \right)
\tag{2.4}\] By strictly quarantining modality \(m\) from contributing to its own target, the optimization landscape precludes trivial self-reconstruction loops and identity memorization.
\(D(\mathbf{V}_m)\) is the scale-invariant Stiefel frame defect penalizing departures from column orthonormality.
\(\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{Z})\) defines joint regularization terms, such as cross-covariance penalties between shared and private partitions.


2.1.3.1 Robust Log-Cosh Negentropy Alignment Functional
The choice of alignment functional \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{align}}\) determines the geometry of cross-modal consensus. While standard Mean Squared Error (MSE) assumes isotropic Gaussian errors, biomedical measurements routinely exhibit heavy-tailed noise and asymmetric clinical outliers. To ensure robust consensus formation, we implement the log-cosh negentropy contrast functional (calculate_ica_energy in src/pysimlr/simlr.py):
\[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{log-cosh}}(\mathbf{Z}_m, \mathbf{U}_{\neq m}) = - \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^k \sum_{j=1}^k \left( |C_{ji}| - \log 2 + \log\left(1 + e^{-2|C_{ji}|}\right) \right)
\tag{2.5}\]
where \(\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{U}_{\neq m}^\top \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times k}\) represents the cross-modal projection matrix with entries \(C_{ji}\), distinct from the underlying biological state \(\mathbf{S}\), and the outer factor \(1/n\) normalizes the sum over latent components by the sample size \(n\) (calculate_ica_energy in src/pysimlr/simlr.py:844-848).
The first-order variational gradient of the loss with respect to the projection basis \(\mathbf{V}_m\) evaluates to (with calculate_ica_gradient returning the corresponding ascent direction \(-\nabla_{\mathbf{V}_m} \mathcal{L}_{\text{log-cosh}}\)):
\[
\nabla_{\mathbf{V}_m} \mathcal{L}_{\text{log-cosh}} = - \frac{1}{n} \mathbf{X}_m^\top \mathbf{U}_{\neq m} \tanh(\mathbf{C})
\tag{2.6}\]
Because the hyperbolic tangent is strictly bounded, \(|\tanh(c)| < 1\) for all \(c \in \mathbb{R}\), the maximum gradient contribution from any single observation or corrupted feature is bounded. This prevents leverage points and extreme phenotypic outliers from destabilizing the shared consensus trajectory.

2.2.6.3 Invertible Affine Coupling and Joint Gaussian Inference
Each view is modeled via an invertible mapping composed of RealNVP affine coupling layers (Dinh et al. 2016; Rezende and Mohamed 2015). For coordinate vector \(\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^k\), a coupling layer splits coordinates using a binary mask \(\mathbf{b} \in \{0, 1\}^k\): \[
\mathbf{z}_1 = \mathbf{b} \odot \mathbf{z}, \quad \mathbf{z}_2 = (1 - \mathbf{b}) \odot \left( \mathbf{z} \odot e^{s(\mathbf{z}_1)} + t(\mathbf{z}_1) \right), \quad \mathbf{z}' = \mathbf{z}_1 + \mathbf{z}_2
\tag{2.9}\] where \(s\) and \(t\) are scaling and translation networks. Scale outputs are bounded via \(s(\mathbf{z}_1) = \text{scale\_bound} \times \tanh(s_{\text{net}}(\mathbf{z}_1))\) to ensure numerical stability. The inverse transformation is analytically exact: \[
\mathbf{z}_1 = \mathbf{b} \odot \mathbf{z}', \quad \mathbf{z}_2 = (1 - \mathbf{b}) \odot \left( (\mathbf{z}' - t(\mathbf{z}_1)) \odot e^{-s(\mathbf{z}_1)} \right), \quad \mathbf{z} = \mathbf{z}_1 + \mathbf{z}_2
\tag{2.10}\] with log-Jacobian determinant \(\log |\det J| = \sum_{j: b_j = 0} s_j(\mathbf{z}_1)\).
Because normalizing flows map empirical data to standard Gaussian latents, the concatenated shared latent space across all views is parameterized as a joint Gaussian: \[
\mathbf{Z}_{\text{joint}} = [\mathbf{Z}_{1,\text{shared}} \parallel \dots \parallel \mathbf{Z}_{M,\text{shared}}] \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \Sigma)
\tag{2.11}\] Partitioning into observed view \(A\) and unobserved view \(B\), the conditional latent mean given observed view \(A\) evaluates via the Schur complement: \[
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{B|A} = \boldsymbol{\mu}_B + \Sigma_{BA} \Sigma_{AA}^{-1} (\mathbf{Z}_{A,\text{shared}} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_A)
\tag{2.12}\] Solved via Cholesky factorization, the conditional coordinates are decoded into ambient space. For Full-Space Flow-SiMR, decoding is evaluated via \(\hat{\mathbf{X}}_B = \text{Flow}_{\psi_B}^{-1}([\boldsymbol{\mu}_{B|A} \parallel \mathbf{0}])\), whereas for Flow-SiMR-V, decoding projects back through the OLEE basis: \(\hat{\mathbf{X}}_B = \text{Flow}_{\psi_B}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{B|A}) \mathbf{V}_B^\top\).

text:
2.3 Manifold Optimization and Algorithmic Mechanics

2.3.1 Stiefel Manifold Optimization and SVD Elimination
The parameter space for each projection basis \(\mathbf{V}_m \in \mathbb{R}^{p_m \times k}\) is the compact Stiefel manifold: \[
\text{St}(k, p_m) = \{ \mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{p_m \times k} \mid \mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{V} = \mathbf{I}_k \}
\tag{2.13}\] In Euclidean gradient descent, unconstrained parameter updates displace iterates off the manifold. Mapping tangent iterates \(\mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{p_m \times k}\) back to \(\text{St}(k, p_m)\) requires a retraction mapping \(R: T \text{St}(k, p_m) \to \text{St}(k, p_m)\).

2.3.1.1 Riemannian Tangent Space and Metric Projections
For an iterate \(\mathbf{V} \in \text{St}(k, p_m)\), the tangent space \(T_{\mathbf{V}} \text{St}(k, p_m)\) comprises all displacement matrices \(\Delta \in \mathbb{R}^{p_m \times k}\) satisfying the linearized orthonormality constraint: \[
T_{\mathbf{V}} \text{St}(k, p_m) = \{ \Delta \in \mathbb{R}^{p_m \times k} \mid \mathbf{V}^\top \Delta + \Delta^\top \mathbf{V} = \mathbf{0} \}
\tag{2.14}\] Under the standard Euclidean metric \(\langle \mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B} \rangle = \text{tr}(\mathbf{A}^\top \mathbf{B})\) inherited from the ambient embedding space \(\mathbb{R}^{p_m \times k}\), the orthogonal projection of an unconstrained ambient gradient \(\mathbf{G} = \nabla_{\mathbf{V}} \mathcal{L}\) onto the tangent space \(T_{\mathbf{V}} \text{St}(k, p_m)\) evaluates in closed form (project_gradient in src/pysimlr/simlr.py:111-146, following Edelman et al. (1998)): \[
\Pi_{T_{\mathbf{V}}}(\mathbf{G}) = \mathbf{G} - \mathbf{V} \, \text{sym}(\mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{G}) = \mathbf{G} - \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{V} (\mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{G} + \mathbf{G}^\top \mathbf{V})
\tag{2.15}\] where \(\text{sym}(\mathbf{M}) = \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{M} + \mathbf{M}^\top)\). (In Grassmann mode, the horizontal tangent projection eliminates the full column space: \(\Pi_{T_{\mathbf{V}}}^{\text{Gr}}(\mathbf{G}) = \mathbf{G} - \mathbf{V}(\mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{G})\).)
The Riemannian gradient is thus given by \(\text{grad}_{\text{St}} \mathcal{L} = \Pi_{T_{\mathbf{V}}}(\nabla_{\mathbf{V}} \mathcal{L})\). Moving along the tangent direction yields an ambient search candidate \(\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{V} - \eta \, \text{grad}_{\text{St}} \mathcal{L}\), which is subsequently mapped back to the manifold via a metric retraction \(R(\mathbf{Y}) \in \text{St}(k, p_m)\).


2.3.1.2 Sylvester Polar Factor Retraction
The canonical metric retraction is the polar factor projection: \[
R(\mathbf{Y}) = \mathbf{Y} (\mathbf{Y}^\top \mathbf{Y})^{-1/2}
\tag{2.16}\] Standard implementations compute \(R(\mathbf{Y}) = \mathbf{U} \mathbf{W}^\top\) via Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), \(\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{U} \Sigma \mathbf{W}^\top\). However, explicit SVD incurs severe computational and numerical pathology:

Branch Divergence & Kernel Serialization: SVD algorithms (e.g. Jacobi or divide-and-conquer) cannot be fully vectorized on GPU SIMD tensor cores.
Singular Value Multiplicity Singularity: The backpropagation derivative of an SVD contains terms proportional to \((\sigma_i^2 - \sigma_j^2)^{-1}\). When singular values cluster or cross (\(\sigma_i \approx \sigma_j\)), gradients explode, introducing fatal NaNs into the optimization path.

To circumvent this, we express the polar factor \(\mathbf{H} = (\mathbf{Y}^\top \mathbf{Y})^{1/2}\) via the continuous Lyapunov/Sylvester system (src/pysimlr/nsa_backend.py:236-254, with SVD fallback in src/pysimlr/sparsification.py:494-510): \[
\mathbf{H} (d\mathbf{H}) + (d\mathbf{H}) \mathbf{H} = d(\mathbf{Y}^\top \mathbf{Y}) = (d\mathbf{Y})^\top \mathbf{Y} + \mathbf{Y}^\top (d\mathbf{Y})
\tag{2.17}\] Because \(\mathbf{H}\) is symmetric positive definite (\(\mathbf{H} \succ 0\)), this Sylvester equation has a provably unique solution \(d\mathbf{H}\). Gradients flow smoothly through backpropagation without encountering eigenvalue multiplicity singularities.


2.3.1.3 Newton-Schulz Cubic Matrix Recurrence and Convergence Proof
To eliminate SVD factorizations entirely from the forward execution loop, we approximate the inverse square root \((\mathbf{Y}^\top \mathbf{Y})^{-1/2}\) via the cubic Newton-Schulz matrix polynomial (src/pysimlr/utils.py:1324-1380): \[
\mathbf{Y}_0 = \frac{\mathbf{Y}}{\|\mathbf{Y}\|_F}, \quad \mathbf{Y}_{\tau+1} = \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{Y}_\tau \left( 3 \mathbf{I}_k - \mathbf{Y}_\tau^\top \mathbf{Y}_\tau \right)
\tag{2.18}\]
Theorem (Quadratic Convergence to the Stiefel Manifold):
Let \(\mathbf{Y}_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times k}\) have singular values \(\sigma_{0, i} \in (0, \sqrt{3})\) for all \(i \in \{1, \dots, k\}\). The sequence of iterates \(\mathbf{Y}_\tau\) converges quadratically to the nearest point on the Stiefel manifold \(\text{St}(k, p)\): \[
\|\mathbf{Y}_{\tau+1}^\top \mathbf{Y}_{\tau+1} - \mathbf{I}_k\| = \mathcal{O}\left(\|\mathbf{Y}_\tau^\top \mathbf{Y}_\tau - \mathbf{I}_k\|^2\right)
\tag{2.19}\]
Proof:
Let the singular value decomposition of iterate \(\tau\) be \(\mathbf{Y}_\tau = \mathbf{P} \Sigma_\tau \mathbf{Q}^\top\), where \(\mathbf{P} \in \text{St}(k, p)\), \(\mathbf{Q} \in \mathbb{O}(k)\), and \(\Sigma_\tau = \text{diag}(\sigma_{\tau, 1}, \dots, \sigma_{\tau, k})\). Substituting this decomposition into the Newton-Schulz recurrence: \[
\mathbf{Y}_{\tau+1} = \frac{1}{2} \left(\mathbf{P} \Sigma_\tau \mathbf{Q}^\top\right) \left( 3 \mathbf{I}_k - \mathbf{Q} \Sigma_\tau^2 \mathbf{Q}^\top \right) = \mathbf{P} \left[ \frac{1}{2} \Sigma_\tau \left( 3 \mathbf{I}_k - \Sigma_\tau^2 \right) \right] \mathbf{Q}^\top
\] Because the singular vectors \(\mathbf{P}\) and \(\mathbf{Q}\) are stationary under the iteration, the matrix recurrence decouples into \(k\) independent scalar recurrences for each singular value \(\sigma_{\tau, i}\): \[
\sigma_{\tau+1, i} = \frac{1}{2} \sigma_{\tau, i} \left( 3 - \sigma_{\tau, i}^2 \right)
\] Define the relative distance to the Stiefel manifold for singular value \(i\) as \(\epsilon_{\tau, i} = 1 - \sigma_{\tau, i}\). Expressing \(\sigma_{\tau, i} = 1 - \epsilon_{\tau, i}\) and expanding: \[
\sigma_{\tau+1, i} = \frac{1}{2}(1 - \epsilon_{\tau, i}) \left( 3 - (1 - \epsilon_{\tau, i})^2 \right)
\] \[
= \frac{1}{2}(1 - \epsilon_{\tau, i}) \left( 3 - (1 - 2\epsilon_{\tau, i} + \epsilon_{\tau, i}^2) \right) = \frac{1}{2}(1 - \epsilon_{\tau, i}) \left( 2 + 2\epsilon_{\tau, i} - \epsilon_{\tau, i}^2 \right)
\] \[
= \frac{1}{2} \left( 2 + 2\epsilon_{\tau, i} - \epsilon_{\tau, i}^2 - 2\epsilon_{\tau, i} - 2\epsilon_{\tau, i}^2 + \epsilon_{\tau, i}^3 \right) = 1 - \frac{3}{2}\epsilon_{\tau, i}^2 + \frac{1}{2}\epsilon_{\tau, i}^3
\] Subtracting both sides from 1 yields the exact recurrence for the error metric: \[
\epsilon_{\tau+1, i} = 1 - \sigma_{\tau+1, i} = \frac{3}{2}\epsilon_{\tau, i}^2 - \frac{1}{2}\epsilon_{\tau, i}^3 = \epsilon_{\tau, i}^2 \left( \frac{3 - \epsilon_{\tau, i}}{2} \right)
\tag{2.20}\] For any \(\sigma_{0, i} \in (0, \sqrt{3})\), \(|\epsilon_{0, i}| < 1\), ensuring monotonic error contraction. As \(\epsilon \to 0\), the cubic term is negligible: \[
\epsilon_{\tau+1} = \frac{3}{2}\epsilon_\tau^2 + \mathcal{O}(\epsilon_\tau^3)
\] Thus, the recurrence converges with quadratic order \(\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^2)\). Because the update requires only matrix multiplications and additions (\(\mathbf{Y}^\top \mathbf{Y}\) and \(\mathbf{Y} \mathbf{M}\)), it compiles directly to hardware tensor cores, achieving zero CPU-GPU transfer bottlenecks. For high-dimensional embeddings (\(k \ge 30\)), where singular values scale as \(\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{k})\), 20 iterations or a spectral norm pre-scaler \(\mathbf{Y}_0 = \mathbf{Y}/\sqrt{\|\mathbf{Y}^\top \mathbf{Y}\|_\infty}\) ensure complete convergence. Geometrical intuition for this orthogonal discovery process is illustrated in Figure 2.7.








Figure 2.7: Geometrical Intuition of Orthogonal Discovery via Stiefel Retraction. Unconstrained deep architectures succumb to latent collapse by entangling redundant variance components (red vectors). Stiefel manifold retractions constrain feature discovery to the orthonormal manifold (wireframe sphere), distilling distinct, statistically independent generative factors (green orthogonal vectors).








2.3.2 Quasi-Newton Curvature Steps via torch_lbfgs
Joint-variational alignment produces an ill-conditioned optimization landscape, characterized by narrow parabolic ravines formed by cross-modal consensus constraints and Stiefel manifold boundaries. Standard first-order stochastic gradient methods (SGD, Adam) suffer from pathological oscillations across ravine walls.
We accelerate convergence by deploying quasi-Newton second-order curvature estimation via torch_lbfgs (src/pysimlr/optimizers.py:841-894). Let \(\mathbf{s}_t = \mathbf{V}_{t+1} - \mathbf{V}_t\) denote the parameter displacement and \(\mathbf{y}_t = \nabla \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{V}_{t+1}) - \nabla \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{V}_t)\) denote the gradient variation. Over a rolling history of size \(h=10\), the inverse Hessian approximation \(\mathbf{H}_t \approx \nabla^2 \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{V}_t)^{-1}\) is computed via the two-loop recursion:

Backward History Loop: Initialize \(\mathbf{q} = \nabla \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{V}_t)\). For \(i = t-1\) down to \(t-h\): \[
\alpha_i = \rho_i \text{tr}(\mathbf{s}_i^\top \mathbf{q}), \quad \mathbf{q} \leftarrow \mathbf{q} - \alpha_i \mathbf{y}_i, \quad \text{where } \rho_i = \frac{1}{\text{tr}(\mathbf{y}_i^\top \mathbf{s}_i)}
\]
Initial Scaling: \(\mathbf{r} = \gamma_t \mathbf{q}\), with \(\gamma_t = \frac{\text{tr}(\mathbf{s}_{t-1}^\top \mathbf{y}_{t-1})}{\text{tr}(\mathbf{y}_{t-1}^\top \mathbf{y}_{t-1})}\).
Forward History Loop: For \(i = t-h\) up to \(t-1\): \[
\beta = \rho_i \text{tr}(\mathbf{y}_i^\top \mathbf{r}), \quad \mathbf{r} \leftarrow \mathbf{r} + \mathbf{s}_i (\alpha_i - \beta)
\]
Descent Direction: The update step is \(\mathbf{p}_t = -\mathbf{r}\), accepted under Strong Wolfe line search conditions: \[
\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{V}_t + \alpha_t \mathbf{p}_t) \le \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{V}_t) + c_1 \alpha_t \text{tr}(\nabla \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{V}_t)^\top \mathbf{p}_t)
\tag{2.21}\] \[
|\text{tr}(\nabla \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{V}_t + \alpha_t \mathbf{p}_t)^\top \mathbf{p}_t)| \le c_2 |\text{tr}(\nabla \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{V}_t)^\top \mathbf{p}_t)|
\]


2.3.2.1 Analytical Gradient Closures
In PyTorch’s native optim.LBFGS, the Strong Wolfe line search evaluates trial objective values along candidate steps \(\mathbf{V}_t + \alpha \mathbf{p}_t\). Because SiMLR relies on exact analytical gradients rather than automatic differentiation, caching a static gradient at step entry causes trial evaluations to use stale directions, degrading the curvature estimate. We implement an analytical callback closure:
def closure():
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    with torch.no_grad():
        v_param.grad = -grad_fn(v_param.detach()).contiguous()
        loss = full_energy_function(v_param.detach())
    return torch.as_tensor(float(loss), device=v_param.device)
This guarantees that second-order curvature approximations remain mathematically exact throughout the line search, enabling SiMLR-LBFGSB to achieve the best overall Friedman rank (\(3.28\)) and highest sparse support recovery (\(0.942\)) across the 9-dataset (243-evaluation) benchmark while SiMLR-LBFGS converges in \(0.175\text{s}\).



2.3.3 Scale-Invariant Frame Defect and Squared-Cosine Angle Defect
To regularize the projection basis toward mutual orthogonality without distorting data variance, we evaluate two complementary geometric metrics: the trace-normalized Stiefel frame defect \(D(\mathbf{V})\) and the squared-cosine angle defect \(C(\mathbf{V})\).

2.3.3.1 Trace-Normalized Stiefel Frame Defect (\(D\))
The trace-normalized frame defect (src/pysimlr/utils.py:504-630) measures departure from uniform Stiefel projection: \[
D(\mathbf{V}) = \frac{1}{1 - 1/k} \left\| \frac{\mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{V}}{\text{tr}(\mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{V})} - \frac{1}{k} \mathbf{I}_k \right\|_F^2
\tag{2.22}\] Let \(\mathbf{G} = \mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times k}\) denote the unnormalized Gram matrix and let \(t = \text{tr}(\mathbf{G}) = \|\mathbf{V}\|_F^2\). The normalized Gram matrix is \(\tilde{\mathbf{G}} = \frac{\mathbf{G}}{t}\). Expanding the Frobenius norm: \[
\|\tilde{\mathbf{G}} - \frac{1}{k} \mathbf{I}_k\|_F^2 = \sum_{i \ne j} \tilde{G}_{ij}^2 + \sum_{i=1}^k \left( \tilde{G}_{ii} - \frac{1}{k} \right)^2
\] The first summation measures column decorrelation, while the second summation penalizes departures from norm balance (\(\tilde{G}_{ii} = 1/k\)). Because the participation ratio is \(\text{EffRank}(\mathbf{V}) = \frac{t^2}{\|\mathbf{G}\|_F^2}\), the frame defect connects directly to effective rank: \[
D(\mathbf{V}) = \frac{1}{1 - 1/k} \left( \frac{1}{\text{EffRank}(\mathbf{V})} - \frac{1}{k} \right)
\] Differentiating with respect to \(\mathbf{V}\) gives the closed-form gradient: \[
\nabla_{\mathbf{V}} D(\mathbf{V}) = \frac{4}{t^2 (1 - 1/k)} \left[ \mathbf{V} \mathbf{G} - \frac{\|\mathbf{G}\|_F^2}{t} \mathbf{V} \right]
\tag{2.23}\] Because \(D(\mathbf{V})\) is degree-0 homogeneous, \(\langle \nabla_{\mathbf{V}} D(\mathbf{V}), \mathbf{V} \rangle \equiv 0\) (Euler’s theorem). The defect gradient exerts zero radial force on matrix scale, acting purely as a shape-conforming projection.


2.3.3.2 Squared-Cosine Angle Defect (\(C\))
While \(D(\mathbf{V})\) enforces strict orthonormality (decorrelation plus equal column norms), biological signals frequently exhibit heterogeneous variance hierarchies across components. Demanding equal column lengths (\(\tilde{G}_{ii} = 1/k\)) penalizes true non-negative components: a perfectly disjoint non-negative basis whose parts differ in magnitude scores \(D > 0.20\) rather than zero.
To penalize departures from mutual orthogonality invariant to per-column scaling, we implement the squared-cosine angle defect (angle_defect in src/pysimlr/utils.py:633-724), with \(\mathbf{U} = \mathbf{V} \text{diag}(\|\mathbf{v}_1\|_2^{-1}, \dots, \|\mathbf{v}_k\|_2^{-1})\) (norms floored at \(\epsilon = 10^{-12}\)): \[
C(\mathbf{V}) = \frac{\|\mathbf{U}^\top \mathbf{U} - \mathbf{I}_k\|_F^2}{k(k - 1)}
\tag{2.24}\] Unlike globally trace-normalized off-diagonal defects—which score a rank-collapsed matrix with \(k-1\) zero columns at \(0.0\)—comparing \(\mathbf{U}^\top \mathbf{U}\) against \(\mathbf{I}_k\) charges any floored dead column \(1/(k(k-1))\) while remaining invariant to arbitrary positive column rescalings: \[
\nabla_{\mathbf{V}} C(\mathbf{V}) = \frac{4}{k(k - 1)} \left[ \mathbf{U} \mathbf{H} - \mathbf{U} \, \text{diag}\left(\text{rowsum}(\mathbf{H}^{\odot 2})\right) \right] \text{diag}(\|\mathbf{v}_1\|_2^{-1}, \dots, \|\mathbf{v}_k\|_2^{-1}), \quad \mathbf{H} = \mathbf{U}^\top \mathbf{U} - \mathbf{I}_k
\tag{2.25}\] For non-negative representations \(\mathbf{V} \ge 0\) with non-zero columns, \(C(\mathbf{V}) = 0\) if and only if the columns have pairwise disjoint supports, providing a column-scale-invariant variational diagnostic for non-negative feature clustering.



2.3.4 Support Consolidation and Direct SVD Contrast Splitting
In biological systems, features exhibit bidirectional responses (e.g., regional atrophy versus ventricular expansion). To discover signed components while preserving non-negative interpretability, we lift each basis \(\mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times k}\) into paired non-negative lobes: \[
\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{V}^+ - \mathbf{V}^-, \quad \mathbf{V}^+ = \max(\mathbf{V}, \mathbf{0}), \quad \mathbf{V}^- = \max(-\mathbf{V}, \mathbf{0})
\tag{2.26}\] forming the non-negative matrix \(\mathbf{W} = [\mathbf{V}^+ \mid \mathbf{V}^-] \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times 2k}\).

2.3.4.1 Direct SVD Contrast Initialization
Legacy implementations initialized non-negative signed flows via a 9-stage penalty continuation homotopy (\(\mu \in [0, 10^4]\)), requiring hundreds of iterations and causing execution bottlenecks. On zero-mean centered or signed data, we replace this homotopy with Direct SVD Contrast Splitting: \[
\mathbf{E} = \text{SVD}_k(\mathbf{X}), \quad \mathbf{W}_0 = [\max(\mathbf{E}, \mathbf{0}) \mid \max(-\mathbf{E}, \mathbf{0})]
\tag{2.27}\] Because the data is centered, the leading eigenvectors \(\mathbf{E}\) possess zero column sums and symmetric positive/negative mass. The lifted lobes \(\mathbf{W}_0\) provide an exact subspace initialization (\(\mathbf{V}_0^+ - \mathbf{V}_0^- = \mathbf{E}\)) with zero initial crosstalk (\(\mathbf{V}_0^+ \odot \mathbf{V}_0^- = \mathbf{0}\)). For uncentered non-negative data (\(\mathbf{X} \ge 0\)), an adaptive two-stage continuation seeds both lobes, preventing boundary stalls. This direct splitting yields a 157.7× wall-clock acceleration (from 5.33s to 0.034s per fit).


2.3.4.2 The Support Consolidation Operator
Following continuous optimization at \(w=0.5\), we apply the deterministic support consolidation operator \(\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{V}^+, \mathbf{V}^-)\) to eliminate trailing numerical tails: \[
\text{win}(j) = \arg\max_{l \in \{1, \dots, 2k\}} W_{j, l}
\tag{2.28}\] Each feature \(j\) is assigned strictly to its dominant component lobe and zeroed in all other channels, followed by a brief constrained polish with supports fixed. This guarantees:

Zero Lobe Crosstalk: \(\|\mathbf{V}^+ \odot \mathbf{V}^-\|_1 = 0.0000\).
Exact Disjoint Sparsity: Features map unambiguously to positive or negative axes without attribution leakage.
Exact Manifold Invariance: \(D(\mathbf{V}) = 0.0000\) and \(C(\mathbf{V}) = 0.0000\).




2.3.5 Consensus, Spectral Triage, and Gating Warmup

2.3.5.1 Block-Coordinate Descent and LOO Topology
We formalize optimization through Block-Coordinate Descent (BCD). At each iteration \(t\):

Consensus Formation (LOO Topology): Fixing network parameters \(\{f_m, g_m\}\), consensus targets \(\mathbf{U}_{\neq m}\) are computed strictly excluding modality \(m\): \[
\mathbf{U}_{\neq m}^{(t)} = \text{Consensus}(\{\mathbf{Z}_j^{(t-1)}\}_{j \neq m})
\] This prevents high-capacity encoders from memorizing trivial self-mappings.
Parameter Update: Fixing \(\mathbf{U}_{\neq m}^{(t)}\), each modality minimizes its local variational loss: \[
\{f_m^{(t)}, g_m^{(t)}\} = \arg\min_{f_m, g_m} \mathcal{L}(\{f_m, g_m\}, \mathbf{U}_{\neq m}^{(t)})
\]



2.3.5.2 Sign-Aligned Newton-Schulz Polar Consensus Mixing
In multi-view representation learning, latent factorizations are mathematically invariant under coordinate sign reflections (\(\mathbf{z}_j \leftrightarrow -\mathbf{z}_j\)): if latent vector \(\mathbf{u}_l\) explains a modality, then \(-\mathbf{u}_l\) with negated loadings \(\mathbf{v}_l\) provides an identical physical reconstruction. When integrating multiple observational domains, two views can recover identical underlying biological factors with diametrically opposite signs (e.g., empirical inner-product correlations of \(r = -0.927\) and \(-0.959\)).

2.3.5.2.1 The Destructive Cancellation Failure Mode
Under antipodal sign alignment, naive cross-modal averaging induces catastrophic destructive cancellation: \[
\bar{\mathbf{u}}_l = \frac{1}{M-1} \sum_{j \ne m} \mathbf{z}_{j, l} \approx \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{u}_l - \mathbf{u}_l) = \mathbf{0}
\tag{2.29}\] As quantified in src/pysimlr/utils.py:2003-2064 on planted multi-view benchmarks, unaligned averaging collapses latent column standard deviations from \(\sim 1.0\) down to \(0.121\), precipitating a catastrophic collapse in downstream consensus predictive fidelity from \(R^2 = 0.795\) to \(R^2 = 0.023\). This pathology is silent, intermittent, and seed-dependent, masquerading as model instability rather than an elementary arithmetic cancellation.


2.3.5.2.2 Greedy Column Sign Alignment
To resolve sign indeterminacy prior to consensus mixing, we implement greedy column-wise sign alignment (align_column_signs in src/pysimlr/utils.py:2003-2064). Taking the first view as an initial reference \(\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{Z}_1\), each subsequent view’s columns are sequentially synchronized against the running coordinate sum: \[
s_{j, l} = \text{sign}\left( \sum_{i=1}^n Z_{j, il} R_{il} \right), \quad \tilde{\mathbf{Z}}_j = \mathbf{Z}_j \, \text{diag}(s_{j, 1}, \dots, s_{j, k})
\tag{2.30}\] \[
\mathbf{R} \leftarrow \mathbf{R} + \tilde{\mathbf{Z}}_j
\] Because the sign operators \(s_{j, l}\) are detached from the computational graph, this alignment constitutes a coordinate relabeling that leaves gradient magnitudes intact while eliminating destructive cancellation.


2.3.5.2.3 Newton-Schulz Polar Orthogonalization
Following greedy sign alignment, PySIMLR computes the Leave-One-Out consensus \(\mathbf{U}_{\neq m}\) using sign-aligned Newton-Schulz polar orthogonalization as its default mixing mechanism (mixing_algorithm="newton" in src/pysimlr/consensus.py:121-124): \[
\bar{\mathbf{U}}_{\neq m} = \frac{1}{M-1} \sum_{j \ne m} \tilde{\mathbf{Z}}_j
\] \[
\mathbf{U}_{\neq m} = \text{NewtonSchulz}\left( \bar{\mathbf{U}}_{\neq m}, \text{iterations}=10 \right)
\tag{2.31}\] followed by per-column centering and unit variance standardization (\(\text{std}(\mathbf{U}_{\neq m}) = \mathbf{1}\)). Ten iterations of the cubic Newton-Schulz recurrence ensure exact polar factor orthonormality without invoking GPU-serializing SVD kernels. Furthermore, in online deep consensus training with an exponential running anchor buffer \(\mathbf{A}\), align_anchor_columns (src/pysimlr/consensus.py:9-45) synchronizes the signs of freshly computed consensus batches against \(\mathbf{A}\) prior to EMA accumulation: \[
\mathbf{A}^{(t)} = 0.9 \, \mathbf{A}^{(t-1)} + 0.1 \left( \mathbf{A}_{\text{new}} \odot \text{signs} \right)
\tag{2.32}\] preventing destructive anchor decay across training epochs.



2.3.5.3 Spectral Triage and Modality Alignment Index (MAI)
The mathematical foundation for distinguishing informative biological signal from unstructured bulk noise via spectral sharpness is illustrated in Figure 2.8.








Figure 2.8: Spectral Sharpness as an Exact Discriminant of Modality Fidelity. True generative signal manifests as rank-1 perturbations that break the Marchenko-Pastur bulk distribution limit (gray span). Informative modalities (green) exhibit significant spectral sharpness, escaping the bulk limit to dominate the leading singular values. Conversely, structureless isotropic noise modalities (orange) remain entirely trapped within the analytically derived Marchenko-Pastur threshold, guaranteeing their rigorous mathematical exclusion via the Modality Alignment Index (MAI).





In high-dimensional multi-modal integration, unconstrained cross-covariance yields spurious alignments between unstructured noise views and the shared consensus. Rather than unnormalized Euclidean residual distances—which, when \(\mathbf{Z}_m\) and \(\mathbf{U}_{\neq m}\) are normalized to unit Frobenius norm, expand to \(2 - 2 \sum_{i=1}^k \sigma_i\) and clamp to exactly zero whenever \(\sum \sigma_i < 0.5\) (rendering dynamic weighting inert across typical benchmarks)—we quantify modality fidelity via the Scale-Profiled Procrustes \(R^2\) (src/pysimlr/deep.py:839-869 and src/pysimlr/flows.py:376-407): \[
R_m^2 = \left( \sum_{i=1}^k \sigma_i(\mathbf{Z}_m^\top \mathbf{U}_{\neq m}) \right)^2 \in [0, 1]
\tag{2.33}\] This represents the squared cosine between the optimally rotated and scaled latent representations \(\mathbf{Z}_m\) and \(\mathbf{U}_{\neq m}\). It is smoothly bounded in \([0, 1]\) and strictly non-zero (\(0.989\) for informative biological signal versus \(0.020\) for pure noise).
To rigorously penalize isotropic noise views that lack internal coordinate structure, we modulate \(R_m^2\) by the Spectral Sharpness \(\mathcal{S}_m = \sigma_1(\mathbf{Z}_m) / \sum_{j=1}^k \sigma_j(\mathbf{Z}_m)\): \[
\text{MAI}_m = R_m^2 \cdot \mathcal{S}_m
\tag{2.34}\] Under the Baik-Ben Arous-Péché (BBP) phase transition theorem (Baik et al. 2005), isotropic noise remains trapped within the Marchenko-Pastur bulk (\(\mathcal{S}_m \approx 1/k\)), driving \(\text{MAI}_m \to 0\), whereas structured biological signal spikes (\(\mathcal{S}_m \to 1\)).


2.3.5.4 Exponential Moving Average, Sigmoid Outlier Gating, and Continuous Warmup
Raw alignment indices are stabilized across training epochs via Exponential Moving Average (EMA): \[
\mathbf{mai}^{(t)} = 0.9 \, \mathbf{mai}^{(t-1)} + 0.1 \, \mathbf{mai}_{\text{raw}}^{(t)}
\tag{2.35}\] To prevent premature view suppression (Weight Collapse) during early exploration while squashing severe noise outliers, modality weights are modulated by an adaptive sigmoid outlier gate \(\omega_m^{\text{gate}}\) centered at the modality mean: \[
\mu_{\text{mai}} = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{j=1}^M \text{mai}_j^{(t)}, \quad \kappa = 5.0 + 10.0 \cdot \min\left(1.0, \frac{t}{30}\right)
\] \[
\omega_m^{\text{gate}} = \sigma\left( \kappa \cdot (\text{mai}_m^{(t)} - \mu_{\text{mai}}) \right) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\left(-\kappa (\text{mai}_m^{(t)} - \mu_{\text{mai}})\right)}
\tag{2.36}\] Target weights proportional to the gated alignment are normalized: \[
\tilde{w}_m = \text{mai}_m^{(t)} \cdot \omega_m^{\text{gate}}, \quad w_m^{\text{target}} = \frac{\tilde{w}_m}{\sum_{j=1}^M \tilde{w}_j + 10^{-8}}
\tag{2.37}\] Rather than an abrupt discontinuous step at a fixed epoch threshold, the architecture transitions continuously from uniform weighting \(\mathbf{w}_{\text{uniform}} = [1/M, \dots, 1/M]^\top\) to the target weights via a continuous linear ramp schedule: \[
T_{\text{warm}} = 0.33 \times T_{\text{total}}, \quad \rho = \text{clip}\left( \frac{t - T_{\text{warm}}}{T_{\text{warm}}}, 0.0, 1.0 \right)
\] \[
\mathbf{w}^{(t)} = (1 - \rho) \mathbf{w}_{\text{uniform}} + \rho \mathbf{w}^{\text{target}}
\tag{2.38}\] This guarantees that all modalities contribute equally during initial manifold representation learning, activating dynamic modality triage only once the shared consensus geometry has stabilized.

2.4 Theoretical Properties and Diagnostic Invariants

2.4.1 Mechanistic Auditability via OLEE and Closed-Form Counterfactuals
Standard post-hoc explainability techniques (SHAP, LIME, Integrated Gradients) construct local linear approximations around non-linear neural networks. In high-dimensional biomedical regimes, these approximations are non-unique, highly sensitive to background reference choices, and vulnerable to adversarial gradient noise.
We resolve the “transparency penalty” at the architectural entrypoint via the Only Linear Encoder Entrypoint (OLEE) constraint: \[
\mathbf{Z}_m = \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m, \quad \mathbf{V}_m \in \text{St}(k, p_m), \quad \mathbf{V}_m^\top \mathbf{V}_m = \mathbf{I}_k
\tag{2.39}\] All non-linear operations are strictly delegated downstream to decoders (LEND) or latent normalizing flows (Flow-SiMR-V). This structural information bottleneck establishes three exact mathematical auditability guarantees:

Exact Feature Attribution & Constant Input Gradient: The latent score \(z_{i, l}\) for subject \(i\) on component \(l\) is strictly the linear dot product \(\sum_{j=1}^{p_m} X_{i, j} V_{j, l}\). Feature importance is exact, sample-specific, and requires zero heuristic approximation. Furthermore, the directional derivative of representations with respect to input observations is strictly constant: \[
\nabla_{\mathbf{X}_m} \mathbf{Z}_m = \mathbf{V}_m
\tag{2.40}\] Because this input gradient is independent of the input \(\mathbf{X}_m\), the sensitivity profile is invariant across subjects, preventing gradient saturation, adversarial perturbations, and vanishing attribution artifacts that plague deep non-linear encoders.
Global Variance Partitioning: Because \(\mathbf{V}_m^\top \mathbf{V}_m = \mathbf{I}_k\), the projection is an isometry on \(\mathbb{R}^k\). The total explained variance decomposes additively across orthogonal axes: \(\text{Var}(\mathbf{Z}_m) = \sum_{l=1}^k \text{Var}(\mathbf{z}_{m, l})\).
Closed-Form Minimum-Norm Counterfactuals: Targeted counterfactual state transitions can be evaluated analytically in closed form without iterative gradient search or surrogate sampling, as established by the following theorem.


2.4.1.1 Theorem: Closed-Form Minimum-Norm Counterfactuals
Theorem:
Let a subject have latent representation \(\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{x} \mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^k\) under the OLEE basis \(\mathbf{V} \in \text{St}(k, p)\). To transition the subject to a targeted counterfactual latent state \(\mathbf{z}^* = \mathbf{z} + \Delta \mathbf{z}\), the unique perturbation \(\delta \mathbf{x}^* \in \mathbb{R}^p\) that minimizes the Euclidean intervention effort \(\|\delta \mathbf{x}\|_2^2\) while satisfying \((\mathbf{x} + \delta \mathbf{x}) \mathbf{V} = \mathbf{z}^*\) is given analytically by: \[
\delta \mathbf{x}^* = \Delta \mathbf{z} \mathbf{V}^\top
\tag{2.41}\]
Proof:
The counterfactual perturbation problem is formulated as the constrained optimization: \[
\min_{\delta \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^p} \frac{1}{2} \|\delta \mathbf{x}\|_2^2 \quad \text{subject to} \quad \delta \mathbf{x} \mathbf{V} = \Delta \mathbf{z}
\tag{2.42}\] Introducing Lagrange multipliers \(\boldsymbol{\lambda} \in \mathbb{R}^k\), the Lagrangian is: \[
\mathcal{L}(\delta \mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\lambda}) = \frac{1}{2} \delta \mathbf{x} \delta \mathbf{x}^\top - (\delta \mathbf{x} \mathbf{V} - \Delta \mathbf{z}) \boldsymbol{\lambda}
\] Setting the gradient with respect to \(\delta \mathbf{x}\) to zero: \[
\nabla_{\delta \mathbf{x}} \mathcal{L} = \delta \mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\lambda}^\top \mathbf{V}^\top = \mathbf{0} \implies \delta \mathbf{x} = \boldsymbol{\lambda}^\top \mathbf{V}^\top
\] Multiplying both sides on the right by \(\mathbf{V}\) and enforcing the constraint: \[
\delta \mathbf{x} \mathbf{V} = \boldsymbol{\lambda}^\top \mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{V} = \Delta \mathbf{z}
\] Because \(\mathbf{V}\) lies on the Stiefel manifold, \(\mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{V} = \mathbf{I}_k\). Thus: \[
\boldsymbol{\lambda}^\top \mathbf{I}_k = \Delta \mathbf{z} \implies \boldsymbol{\lambda} = \Delta \mathbf{z}^\top
\] Substituting \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}^\top = \Delta \mathbf{z}\) back into the stationarity equation yields: \[
\delta \mathbf{x}^* = \Delta \mathbf{z} \mathbf{V}^\top
\] The minimum-norm perturbation is closed-form, unique, and requires no iterative gradient search or surrogate sampling.



2.4.2 Subspace vs. Basis Axis Disentanglement
A fundamental methodological challenge in representation learning is separating subspace quality from basis axis interpretability. Downstream evaluations frequently conflate these two concepts:

2.4.2.1 Theorem: Rotation Invariance of Linear Probes
Theorem:
Let \(\mathbf{Z}_1 = \mathbf{X} \mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}\) and let \(\mathbf{M} \in \text{GL}(k, \mathbb{R})\) be an arbitrary invertible \(k \times k\) matrix defining an alternative basis \(\mathbf{Z}_2 = \mathbf{X} \mathbf{V} \mathbf{M} = \mathbf{Z}_1 \mathbf{M}\). For any regression target \(\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}\):

The Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) projection hat matrices are identical: \(\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{Z}_2} \equiv \mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{Z}_1}\).
The fitted values and regression \(R^2\) are strictly invariant: \(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_2 \equiv \hat{\mathbf{y}}_1\) and \(R^2(\mathbf{Z}_2, \mathbf{y}) \equiv R^2(\mathbf{Z}_1, \mathbf{y})\).

Proof:
The OLS hat matrix projecting \(\mathbf{y}\) onto the column space of \(\mathbf{Z}_2\) is: \[
\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{Z}_2} = \mathbf{Z}_2 \left( \mathbf{Z}_2^\top \mathbf{Z}_2 \right)^{-1} \mathbf{Z}_2^\top
\tag{2.43}\] Substituting \(\mathbf{Z}_2 = \mathbf{Z}_1 \mathbf{M}\): \[
\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{Z}_2} = (\mathbf{Z}_1 \mathbf{M}) \left( (\mathbf{Z}_1 \mathbf{M})^\top (\mathbf{Z}_1 \mathbf{M}) \right)^{-1} (\mathbf{Z}_1 \mathbf{M})^\top = \mathbf{Z}_1 \mathbf{M} \left( \mathbf{M}^\top (\mathbf{Z}_1^\top \mathbf{Z}_1) \mathbf{M} \right)^{-1} \mathbf{M}^\top \mathbf{Z}_1^\top
\] Because \(\mathbf{M}\) is invertible, \((\mathbf{A} \mathbf{B} \mathbf{C})^{-1} = \mathbf{C}^{-1} \mathbf{B}^{-1} \mathbf{A}^{-1}\): \[
\mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{Z}_2} = \mathbf{Z}_1 \mathbf{M} \mathbf{M}^{-1} \left( \mathbf{Z}_1^\top \mathbf{Z}_1 \right)^{-1} (\mathbf{M}^\top)^{-1} \mathbf{M}^\top \mathbf{Z}_1^\top = \mathbf{Z}_1 \mathbf{I}_k \left( \mathbf{Z}_1^\top \mathbf{Z}_1 \right)^{-1} \mathbf{I}_k \mathbf{Z}_1^\top = \mathbf{Z}_1 \left( \mathbf{Z}_1^\top \mathbf{Z}_1 \right)^{-1} \mathbf{Z}_1^\top = \mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{Z}_1}
\] The predicted values are \(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_2 = \mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{Z}_2} \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{H}_{\mathbf{Z}_1} \mathbf{y} = \hat{\mathbf{y}}_1\). The regression coefficients simply absorb the transformation: \(\boldsymbol{\beta}_2 = \mathbf{M}^{-1} \boldsymbol{\beta}_1\).


2.4.2.2 Coordinate Sensitivity of Tree Ensembles
In sharp contrast to linear probes, decision trees in a Random Forest recursively split data along coordinate-aligned hyperplanes: \[
\mathcal{H}_{l, \theta} = \{ \mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^k \mid z_l \le \theta \}
\tag{2.44}\] Under a generic rotation \(\mathbf{M}\), each coordinate becomes an oblique linear combination \(z_l' = \sum_{j=1}^k M_{jl} z_j\). To isolate rotated patterns, axis-aligned trees require an exponential cascade of staircase splits, degrading generalization performance.


2.4.2.3 The Dual-Probe Diagnostic
Consequently, downstream evaluations must deploy a dual-probe protocol:

Linear Probe (OLS / Logistic Regression): Quantifies subspace recovery. Performance is completely invariant to basis rotation (\(\Delta R^2 = 0.0000\)).
Tree Probe (Random Forest): Quantifies coordinate axis alignment, non-negativity, and sparsity.

A performance difference observed in tree probes accompanied by a tie in linear probes localizes the effect specifically to coordinate axis disentanglement rather than subspace capture.



2.4.3 Theoretical Bounds: The 1/M Law
Let each modality observation \(\mathbf{X}_m\) be generated by a shared true manifold embedded in additive Gaussian noise with noise variance \(\sigma^2\) and cross-modal correlation \(\rho\). Aggregating observations across \(M\) modalities yields the consensus estimator variance: \[
\text{Var}(\mathbf{U}) = \frac{\sigma^2}{M} (1 - \rho) + \rho \sigma^2
\tag{2.45}\] As \(M \to \infty\), the independent noise term \(\frac{\sigma^2}{M}(1-\rho)\) vanishes. Consequently, the irreducible error floor is strictly bounded by \(\rho \sigma^2\). While expanding \(M\) mitigates independent noise, it cannot resolve correlated cross-modal artifacts, necessitating the LOO topology and Spectral Triage to actively suppress correlated noise components.

2.5.2 Statistical Determination of Intrinsic Dimensionality (\(k\))
We implement three statistical strategies to establish the optimal latent dimensionality \(k\):

Information Criteria (BIC): Evaluates the Bayesian Information Criterion to penalize excessive model parameterization.
Spectral Truncation (Tracy-Widom): Computes the statistical significance of singular values against the null hypothesis of purely unstructured noise.

3.1.1 Multi-Modal Data Regimes and Replication Structure
To rigorously evaluate multi-modal architectures across distinct inductive biases and biomedical domains, we establish a comprehensive benchmark protocol across 9 multi-modal data regimes (6 controlled synthetic manifolds with known ground-truth \(\mathbf{U}^*\) and \(\mathbf{V}^*\), plus 3 public clinical/multi-omics cohorts) evaluated across \(N_{\text{seeds}} = 3\) independent random seeds (\([42, 43, 44]\)) and 9 model architectures (\(243\) total model evaluations, with private_scale = 0.5, consolidate = False, and recommended "pca" initialization), alongside a dedicated 10-seed 4-view neuroimaging mediation benchmark on ADNI-MCI (\(N = 1,084\)). Following Demšar (2006), global statistical inference is conducted on the \(B = 9\) independent dataset blocks (build_ranking_blocks in src/pysimlr/benchmarks/deep_ranking.py), averaging replicates within each dataset before ranking so repeated seeds never inflate degrees of freedom.


3.1.2 Established Real-World Biomedical Cohorts
All real-world cohorts underwent strict in-fold standardization (StandardScaler fitted exclusively on the training partition) to prevent test-set leakage:

Cleveland Heart Disease (Heart, \(N=297\), 2 views: \(p_1=7, p_2=6\)):

Cohort Source & Filtering: Drawn from the UCI Machine Learning Repository (processed.cleveland.data, cached locally at data/heart_cleveland.csv) (Detrano et al. 1989). From the 303 clinical records, six individuals with missing values (?) are removed, yielding \(N=297\) complete records.
View Partitioning: Clinical predictors are split into two diagnostic views:

\(V_1\) (\(p_1=7\)): Resting clinical history and vitals (age, sex, chest pain type cp, resting blood pressure trestbps, serum cholesterol chol, fasting blood sugar fbs, resting ECG restecg).
\(V_2\) (\(p_2=6\)): Exercise stress testing and fluoroscopy (maximum heart rate thalach, exercise-induced angina exang, ST depression oldpeak, peak exercise ST slope slope, major vessels colored by fluoroscopy ca, thallium scintigraphy thal).

Downstream Task & Results: Binary coronary artery disease diagnosis (num > 0, majority rate \(53.9\%\)). In the 3-seed benchmark, NSAFlow-PCA and PCA achieve \(83.7\%\) test accuracy (\(84.8\%\) strictly linear probe for NSAFlow-PCA), followed by LEND, NED, SiMLR, and SiMLR-LBFGSB at \(83.0\%\text{–}83.3\%\).

Diabetes Progression (Diabetes, \(N=442\), 2 views: \(p_1=5, p_2=5\)):

Cohort Source: The Efron et al. clinical diabetes cohort (Efron et al. 2004) (sklearn.datasets.load_diabetes).
View Partitioning: Ten baseline predictors are partitioned into patient/hemodynamic measures and serum panel chemistries:

\(V_1\) (\(p_1=5\)): Patient demographics, anthropometrics, and total cholesterol (age, sex, bmi, mean blood pressure bp, total serum cholesterol s1).
\(V_2\) (\(p_2=5\)): Specialized blood serum panel (LDL s2, HDL s3, total/HDL ratio s4, log triglycerides s5, fasting glucose s6).

Downstream Task & Results: Continuous 1-year disease progression (\(R^2\)). In the 3-seed benchmark, NSAFlow-PCA leads global consensus prediction (\(R^2 = 0.382\)), followed by SiMLR-LBFGS (\(R^2 = 0.352\)), PCA (\(R^2 = 0.350\)), and LEND (\(R^2 = 0.346\)), while SiMLR-LBFGSB achieves the highest strictly linear (\(R^2 = 0.396\)) and axis-sensitive (\(R^2 = 0.355\)) first-layer probe scores.

TCGA-BRCA 3-View Multi-Omics (MultiOmics, \(N=822\), 3 views: \(p=[200, 150, 150]\)):

Cohort Source: The Cancer Genome Atlas Breast Invasive Carcinoma cohort (data/tcga/BRCA_*, cached at data/tcga/brca_er_cached.npz) (The Cancer Genome Atlas Network 2012; Cancer Discovery 2016).
View Partitioning: Three distinct molecular assay platforms across \(N=822\) primary tumors with complete multi-omic profiles and adjudicated receptor status:

\(V_1\) (\(p_1=200\)): Top-variance mRNA sequencing gene expression transcripts (Illumina HiSeqV2).
\(V_2\) (\(p_2=150\)): Somatic Copy Number Variation (CNV) GISTIC2 gene-level scores.
\(V_3\) (\(p_3=150\)): Reverse Phase Protein Array (RPPA) targeted proteomic and phosphoproteomic markers.

Downstream Task & Results: Binary classification of clinical Estrogen Receptor (ER) status (Positive vs. Negative, ER+ prevalence \(76.4\%\)). In the 3-seed benchmark, NSAFlow-PCA achieves \(92.7\%\) test accuracy, followed by LEND (\(91.9\%\)), PCA (\(91.9\%\)), NEDPP (\(91.8\%\)), and SiMLR-LBFGSB (\(91.7\%\), with \(93.0\%\) strictly linear probe accuracy).

ADNI-MCI 4-View Neurodegeneration Mediation Cohort (\(N=1,084\), 4 views: \(p=[160, 160, 62, 13]\)):

Cohort Source: \(N=1,084\) individuals diagnosed with Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) from the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (Weiner et al. 2017; Jack et al. 2008).
View Partitioning: Three structural brain MRI views (\(382\) features: macro-volume \(p_1=160\), hierarchical cortical thickness \(p_2=160\), native T1w thickness \(p_3=62\)) and one cognitive domain battery (\(p_4=13\) sub-items), adjusting for Age, Sex, and Education.
Downstream Task & Results: Out-of-sample prediction of daily functional disability (CDR-SB) and global cognition (MMSE). Direct brain MRI alone hits a ceiling of \(R^2 = 0.0411\), whereas cognitive mediation boosts prediction more than 6-fold (LEND-SiMR + MAI: \(R^2 = 0.2648 \pm 0.0332\); SiMLR: \(R^2 = 0.2443 \pm 0.0534\) in \(0.86\text{s}\)), detailed in plain language in Section 3.5.

Additional Auxiliary Validation Cohorts (mfeat, ADNI-DX, TCGA-KIRC):

Complementing the primary benchmark, auxiliary evaluations on UCI Multiple Features (mfeat, \(N=2,000, p=[76, 64, 6, 47]\), 10-class digits), 3-class ADNI-DX (\(N=685, p=[300, 145, 36]\)), and TCGA-KIRC (\(N=467, p=[300, 300, 232]\)) confirm that OLEE-constrained models avoid the high-dimensional canonical correlation overfitting seen in unregularized GCCA-raw.

3.1.3 Controlled Synthetic Generative Regimes
To test distinct, non-overlapping hypotheses about multi-view recovery \((\mathbf{U}^*, \mathbf{V}^*)\) under private_scale = 0.5, synthetic_cases.py defines six synthetic generative regimes:

Clean Linear Multi-View Manifold (Linear, \(N=1,000, K=3, p=[100, 80, 60]\)): \[\mathbf{X}_m = \mathbf{U}^* \mathbf{V}_m^\top + \mathbf{U}_{m,\text{priv}} \mathbf{V}_{m,\text{priv}}^\top + \mathbf{E}_m\] where shared latent scales \([1.2, 1.0, 0.85]\) exceed view-private background (\(\sigma_{\text{priv}} = 0.5\)) and Gaussian noise (\(\sigma = 0.5\)), with equal outcome weights \(\mathbf{w} = [1, 1, 1]^\top\). Tests baseline recovery where linear and cross-view models should perform at parity (\(R^2 \approx 0.976\text{–}0.990\)).
Polynomial Latent Warping (Polynomial, \(N=1,000, K=3, p=[120, 80, 50]\)): \[\mathbf{X}_m = \psi_m^{\text{poly}}(\mathbf{U}^*) \mathbf{V}_m^\top + \mathbf{U}_{m,\text{priv}} \mathbf{V}_{m,\text{priv}}^\top + \mathbf{E}_m\] where \(\psi_m^{\text{poly}}(\mathbf{U}^*)\) applies non-cancelling quadratic, cross-product, and cubic distortions in \(\mathbb{R}^k\) prior to linear projection \(\mathbf{V}_m^\top\). Because same-sign quadratic warpings do not cancel when views are averaged linearly, axis-sensitive nonlinear probes on \(\mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m\) (NED \(0.961\), Flow-SiMR-V \(0.954\), LEND \(0.954\)) outperform linear OLS on \(\mathbf{U}\) (\(0.870\text{–}0.874\)).
Sinusoidal Periodic Warping (Sine, \(N=1,000, K=3, p=[120, 80, 50]\)): \[\mathbf{X}_m = \psi_m^{\text{sin}}(\mathbf{U}^*) \mathbf{V}_m^\top + \mathbf{U}_{m,\text{priv}} \mathbf{V}_{m,\text{priv}}^\top + \mathbf{E}_m\] where \(\psi_m^{\text{sin}}(\mathbf{U}^*)\) combines linear coordinates with non-cancelling trigonometric oscillations (\(\sin\) and \(\cos\) couplings). Tests recovery under periodic manifold curvature.
Asymmetric Shared-Plus-Private Manifold (Shared+Private, \(N=1,000, K_{\text{sh}}=3, K_{\text{pr}}=2, p=[160, 60, 30]\)): \[\mathbf{X}_m = \mathbf{U}_{\text{shared}}^* \mathbf{V}_{m, \text{sh}}^\top + \mathbf{U}_{m, \text{pr}}^* \mathbf{V}_{m, \text{pr}}^\top + \mathbf{E}_m\] where shared scales decay (\([1.0, 0.625, 0.455]\)) while the largest view (\(p_1=160\)) carries heightened view-private variance (\(\sigma_{\text{priv},1} = 0.80\)). Single-matrix concatenation (PCA \(R^2 = 0.639\), NSAFlow-PCA \(R^2 = 0.629\)) is pulled toward View 1’s private variance, whereas cross-view consensus in LEND recovers all shared factors (\(R^2 = 0.949\), \(CMC = 0.896\)) and Flow-SiMR-V achieves \(R^2 = 0.908\) on its first-layer linear probe.
Non-Negative Disjoint Parts — Dominant Signal (NonnegParts, \(N=400, K=3, p=[120, 45, 30]\)): Ground-truth loading matrices \(\mathbf{V}_m^* \ge \mathbf{0}\) have strictly disjoint column supports across the \(K=3\) components, and the outcome tracks the dominant shared component (\(u_1^*\)). Bound-constrained SiMLR-LBFGSB recovers the true sparse support with Jaccard score \(0.942\) (followed by LEND at \(0.899\) and Flow-SiMR-V at \(0.883\)), whereas unconstrained PCA scores at the random-partition chance floor (\(0.333\)).
Non-Negative Disjoint Parts — Weak Signal (NonnegPartsWeak, \(N=400, K=3, p=[120, 45, 30]\)): Identical disjoint non-negative basis \(\mathbf{V}_m^*\), but the outcome is driven by the weakest shared component (\(u_3^*\)). Because single-matrix concatenation absorbs view-private noise into its leading components, PCA drops to \(R^2 = 0.522\) and NSAFlow-PCA to \(0.570\), whereas LEND (\(R^2 = 0.732\)), SiMLR-LBFGSB (\(R^2 = 0.715\)), and SiMLR-LBFGS (\(R^2 = 0.706\)) isolate the weak shared component via cross-view alignment and non-negativity.

As reported in Table 3.2 and Figure 3.2:

Box-Constrained Riemannian Solver (SiMLR-LBFGSB, Mean Rank 3.28): Combining L-BFGS-B box constraints with non-negative Stiefel consolidation achieves the best overall predictive rank (\(3.28\), mean predictive score \(0.795 \pm 0.201\), linear probe \(0.830\)) and the highest sparse feature support recovery across the benchmark (\(\text{Support } F_1 = 0.942\)) with near-zero per-view frame defect (\(D = 2 \times 10^{-5}\)).
Linear Encoder with Non-Linear Decoder (LEND, Mean Rank 3.56): LEND achieves the highest mean predictive accuracy (\(0.830 \pm 0.189\)), highest strictly linear probe (\(0.836\)), highest axis-aligned Random Forest probe (\(0.830\)), and highest latent coordinate recovery (\(CMC = 0.907\)). 3.3 Multi-Objective Pareto Frontier Analysis
Architectural selection across clinical and high-dimensional biomedical regimes cannot be reduced to a single 1D predictive metric. Models must be evaluated across four complementary operational axes:

Downstream Predictive Capacity (\(Y\)): Cross-validated out-of-sample \(R^2\) or diagnostic classification accuracy.
Ground-Truth Latent Discovery (\(CMC\) on \(\mathbf{U}\)): Canonical Mean Correlation with the true generative latent coordinates \(\mathbf{S}\).
Sparse Feature Support Recovery (\(F_1\) on \(\mathbf{V}\)): Jaccard/F1 overlap with true localized anatomical or molecular feature blocks, alongside zero signed crosstalk (\(\mathbf{V}^+ \odot \mathbf{V}^- = \mathbf{0}\)).
Computational Throughput (\(t\)): Wall-clock execution time per fit.

LEND leads overall (\(CMC = 0.907\)), especially on Shared+Private (\(0.896\) vs \(0.636\) for PCA) and NonnegParts (\(0.865\) vs \(0.740\) for PCA), while NSAFlow-PCA and PCA reach \(0.992\) on Linear and \(0.936\) on Sine.

In contrast, LEND (\(CMC = 0.896\), test \(R^2 = 0.949\)) and Flow-SiMR-V (\(CMC = 0.692\), linear probe \(R^2 = 0.908\)) isolate the shared cross-view manifold.
