3.5 ADNI-MCI 4-View Mediated Neurodegeneration Benchmark

3.5.1 Why Predicting Clinical Dementia Directly from Brain Scans Hits a Wall
In Alzheimer’s disease and Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), a primary clinical goal is predicting how severely a patient’s day-to-day functioning is impaired, measured by the Clinical Dementia Rating Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB)—a score reflecting whether a person can remember appointments, manage household finances, navigate their neighborhood, and care for themselves.
When researchers train machine learning models to predict CDR-SB directly from structural brain MRI alone, accuracy is consistently disappointing (Jack et al. 2008; Weiner et al. 2017). Across all 382 cortical volume and thickness measurements in our ADNI-MCI cohort (\(N = 1,084\)), predicting CDR-SB directly from brain anatomy reaches an out-of-sample ceiling of only 4.1% explained variance: \[R^2 = 0.0411 \pm 0.0248 \quad (\text{holdout test } R^2 = 4.02\%, \quad \rho = 0.2112, \quad p = 1.2 \times 10^{-4})\]
The reason is simple and biological: a shrinking hippocampus does not directly stop a patient from balancing a checkbook. Instead, Alzheimer’s pathology acts in two sequential steps:

Brain Atrophy \(\to\) Cognitive Loss (Path \(a\)): Physical tissue loss (cortical thinning and volume loss) damages core mental abilities measured in clinic—such as word recall, attention, and spatial orientation.
Cognitive Loss \(\to\) Daily Functional Disability (Path \(b\)): Once those mental abilities decline, the patient loses independence in daily life, driving up their CDR-SB score.



3.5.2 Testing the Two-Step Biological Pathway (Baron–Kenny Mediation)
We tested this two-step pathway across \(N = 1,084\) MCI participants (\(70/30\) train/test split, \(N_{\text{test}} = 326\)) using classical Baron–Kenny mediation and Sobel testing:

Step 1 — Brain Structure Strongly Predicts Cognitive Test Scores (Path \(a\)): \[\alpha = 1.000 \pm 0.081, \quad t = 12.31, \quad p < 10^{-25}, \quad R^2 = 26.13\%, \quad \rho = 0.5335\] Multi-view brain MRI explains over 26% of the variance in domain cognitive performance.
Step 2 — Cognitive Test Scores Directly Drive Daily Disability (Path \(b\)): \[\beta = 0.013 \pm 0.003, \quad t = 4.69, \quad p < 10^{-15}\]
Direct Bypass Path Vanishes (Path \(c'\)): \[\gamma' = 0.002, \quad t = 0.88, \quad p = 0.38 \quad (\text{Not Significant})\] Once cognitive performance is accounted for, the direct link from brain MRI to CDR-SB drops to zero.
Share of the Effect Explained by Mediation: \[PM = \frac{\alpha \beta}{\alpha \beta + \gamma'} = \mathbf{84.5\% - 86.4\%} \quad (\text{Sobel } z = 4.38, \; p < 10^{-15})\]

In plain terms: roughly 85% of the effect of brain atrophy on daily dementia severity flows through cognitive performance. Ignoring this intermediate step is why direct MRI-to-CDR-SB models fail.


3.5.3 4-View Mediated Architecture & 10-Seed Replication Benchmark
To respect this biological cascade, we couple the three structural MRI views with a fourth view containing 13 domain cognitive sub-scores:

\(V_1\): Macro-structural gray matter parcel volumes (\(p_1 = 160\))
\(V_2\): Hierarchical multiscale cortical thickness (\(p_2 = 160\))
\(V_3\): Native T1-weighted cortical thickness (\(p_3 = 62\))
\(V_4\): Domain cognitive battery (\(p_4 = 13\), ADAS-Cog and MMSE sub-items)

All models predict out-of-sample functional disability (CDR-SB) and global cognition (MMSE) after adjusting for age, sex, and education. Table 3.4 reports performance across 10 independent train/test seeds.

title: 4  Discussion
text:
4.1 Non-Parametric Architectural Ranking and Empirical Synthesis
Integrating heterogeneous, high-dimensional observations remains a fundamental task in computational anatomy, neurodegenerative disease modeling, and translational molecular oncology (Stone et al. 2020; Avants et al. 2021). As diagnostic and clinical trial cohorts incorporate multi-sequence structural and diffusion MRI, molecular positron emission tomography, biofluid assays, and high-throughput transcriptomics (Weiner et al. 2017; Jack et al. 2008; Marek et al. 2011), representation learning methods must balance the capacity to model non-linear manifold geometry against the legal, ethical, and scientific necessity for verifiable physical biomarker attribution (Holmberg et al. 2022). In neurotrauma, blast-induced shockwaves produce diffuse microstructural shearing across white matter tracts that demands sparse, signed decomposition without cancellation artifacts (Stone et al. 2024). In cancer genomics, resolving functional oncogenic pathways across somatic copy-number alterations, mRNA expression, and targeted protein arrays in breast carcinoma (BRCA) (The Cancer Genome Atlas Network 2012; Cancer Discovery 2016) and clear cell renal cell carcinoma (KIRC) (The Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network 2013) requires multi-modal alignment that preserves exact gene-level attribution.
In this work, we formulated multi-view representation learning as a constrained variational problem governed by the Only Linear Encoder Entrypoint (OLEE) contract, coupling an initial linear Stiefel projection with downstream Riemannian optimizers, non-linear decoders, and volume-preserving normalizing flows. Through evaluation across 9 distinct data regimes (3 real clinical/genomic cohorts and 6 synthetic manifolds across 3 random seeds, totaling 243 model evaluations), alongside dedicated investigations of 4-view cognitive mediation in Alzheimer’s disease (\(N=1,084\)), we characterize the operational boundaries of multi-modal integration and establish empirical guidelines for biomedical deployment.
Evaluating multi-modal representations requires non-parametric statistical inference that respects dataset-level block structure rather than pooling across replicate seeds (Demšar 2006). Across the \(B = 9\) independent dataset blocks and \(k = 9\) evaluated architectures, the non-parametric Friedman test confirms highly significant performance differences (\(\chi_F^2 = 32.47, p = 7.68 \times 10^{-5}\)), corroborated by the Iman–Davenport extension (\(F_F = 6.57, p = 3.13 \times 10^{-6}\), \(\text{df}_1 = 8, \text{df}_2 = 64\)) (Iman and Davenport 1980). With nine models and nine dataset blocks, the two-tailed Nemenyi Critical Difference at \(\alpha = 0.05\) is \(CD = 4.004\) (Nemenyi 1963), and the median between-model spread-to-noise ratio is \(6.15\times\).
The empirical rankings establish four clear architectural tiers:

Flow-SiMR-V (rank \(6.50\) on \(\mathbf{U}\)) achieves the second-highest strictly linear \(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}\) probe across the entire benchmark (\(0.834\), including \(0.908\) on Shared+Private and \(0.744\) on NonnegPartsWeak) alongside \(0.883\) sparse support recovery and exact analytical invertibility.
Dominated Unconstrained Deep Tier (NED, NEDPP): Fully non-linear autoencoders (NED, rank \(7.72\), \(0.618 \pm 0.227\); NEDPP, rank \(7.83\), \(0.633 \pm 0.249\)) rank last across the benchmark and are significantly outperformed by every OLEE-constrained model under Holm-Bonferroni corrected Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (\(p_{\text{Holm}} \le 0.018\)).

4.2.1 Structure of the Pareto Non-Dominated Set
The empirical results define five distinct operational regimes on the Pareto frontier:

The Predictive and Consensus Discovery Frontier (LEND): Achieving the highest predictive accuracy (\(0.830\)), highest linear probe (\(0.836\)), and highest latent coordinate recovery (\(CMC = 0.907\)), LEND combines a linear Stiefel encoder with a non-linear MLP decoder to isolate shared multi-view structure even when individual views carry heavy private noise (Shared+Private \(R^2 = 0.949\)).
The Sparse Support Localization Frontier (SiMLR-LBFGSB): Achieving the best overall Friedman rank (\(3.28\)) and highest sparse support recovery (\(F_1 = 0.942\)), SiMLR-LBFGSB enforces strict non-negative box constraints alongside Stiefel consolidation (NonnegPartsWeak \(R^2 = 0.715\) vs \(0.522\) for PCA).
The Ultra-Fast Turnkey Sparse Frontier (NSAFlow-PCA): Executing in \(0.029\text{s}\) with \(22.4\%\) disjoint sparsity, NSAFlow-PCA matches PCA (\(0.024\text{s}\)) in speed while outperforming it in predictive accuracy (\(0.782\) vs \(0.774\)) and providing signed, non-cancelling feature lobes.
The Fast Quasi-Newton Frontier (SiMLR-LBFGS): Executing in \(0.175\text{s}\) (\(2\times\) faster than first-order SiMLR), SiMLR-LBFGS delivers \(0.797\) predictive accuracy and \(0.766\) support recovery with Per-view frame defect \(D = 4.7 \times 10^{-4}\).
The Invertible Diffeomorphic Frontier (Flow-SiMR-V): Combining a linear Stiefel entrypoint with bijective RealNVP coupling layers, Flow-SiMR-V achieves \(0.834\) on the strictly linear \(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}\) probe and \(0.883\) support recovery while supporting exact analytical inversion for geodesic trajectory mapping.

title: 4  Discussion
section: 4.3 The Only Linear Encoder Entrypoint (OLEE) and Eliminating the Transparency Penalty
text:
4.3 The Only Linear Encoder Entrypoint (OLEE) and Eliminating the Transparency Penalty
A central design requirement in medical imaging, oncology biomarker discovery, and clinical trials is that representation projections remain verifiable. In standard deep multi-view networks, deeply nested activation functions (\(\mathbf{Z} = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_2 \sigma(\mathbf{W}_1 \mathbf{X} + \mathbf{b}_1) + \mathbf{b}_2)\)) entangle features, precluding direct inspection of how physical measurements relate to latent scores (Rudin 2019). In clinical practice, this incurs an unacceptable transparency penalty: if a latent score stratifies a patient into an aggressive treatment arm, biostatisticians and clinicians must verify whether that score is driven by true anatomical atrophy or batch artifacts (Holmberg et al. 2022).
Post-hoc explainers (such as SHAP and LIME) attempt to circumvent this by querying local surrogate models on randomly perturbed inputs (Ribeiro et al. 2016; Lundberg and Lee 2017). In anatomical and physiological cohorts, post-hoc methods suffer from an out-of-distribution sampling defect: perturbing features independently creates synthetic points that violate physiological covariance (e.g., pairing impossible cortical thickness values or mutually exclusive transcript profiles). This instability can introduce false-positive biomarker attributions (Holmberg et al. 2022; Radulovic 2023).
Deep SiMLR enforces verifiable attribution by restricting the entrypoint of each modality to the Only Linear Encoder Entrypoint (OLEE) contract: \[
\mathbf{Z}_m = \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m, \quad \text{subject to } \mathbf{V}_m \in \text{St}(k, p_m) = \{\mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{p_m \times k} \mid \mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{V} = \mathbf{I}_k\}
\] This architectural contract yields three mathematical and clinical guarantees:

Globally Constant Attribution Gradients: The marginal contribution of feature \(j\) to latent component \(k\) is identically constant across the input domain: \[
\nabla_{\mathbf{X}_m} \mathbf{Z}_m = \mathbf{V}_m, \quad \frac{\partial Z_{m, ik}}{\partial X_{m, ij}} = V_{m, jk}
\] Feature loadings are exact, closed-form, and independent of heuristic perturbation parameters.
Closed-Form Counterfactual Recourse: Determining the minimal physical perturbation \(\delta \mathbf{x}_m\) required to produce a targeted therapeutic shift in latent coordinates \(\Delta \mathbf{z}_m\) reduces to an exact orthogonal projection: \[
\delta \mathbf{x}_m^* = \Delta \mathbf{z}_m \mathbf{V}_m^\top
\] This eliminates iterative gradient searches, non-convex local minima, and off-manifold sampling artifacts, connecting dimensionality reduction directly to actionable causal recourse frameworks (Pearl 2009; Wachter et al. 2017).
Signed Support Consolidation: Decomposing loading matrices into positive and negative lobes (\(\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{V}^+ - \mathbf{V}^-\)) and enforcing disjoint support (\(\mathbf{V}^+ \odot \mathbf{V}^- = \mathbf{0}\)) prevents positive and negative weights from cancelling destructively, ensuring that positive and negative coefficients identify distinct anatomical or biological processes.

title: 4  Discussion
section: 4.4 Why Cognitive Mediation Multiplies ADNI-MCI Prediction by Over 6-Fold
text:
4.4 Why Cognitive Mediation Multiplies ADNI-MCI Prediction by Over 6-Fold
The practical value of the OLEE contract is clearest in our study of \(N = 1,084\) patients with Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) from the ADNI cohort (Weiner et al. 2017; Jack et al. 2008). Clinicians evaluate functional dementia severity using the Clinical Dementia Rating – Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB), which measures how well a patient manages daily life (remembering events, handling household tasks, staying oriented).
Integrating three structural brain MRI views (\(382\) regional volume and cortical thickness measurements) with a fourth view of clinical cognitive tests (\(p_4 = 13\)) reveals three clear findings:

Brain Scans Alone Cannot Predict Daily Disability (\(R^2 \approx 0.041\)): Trying to predict CDR-SB directly from the 382 brain MRI features hits a hard ceiling of only 4.1% explained variance (Direct-Anatomy [SiMLR]: \(R^2 = 0.0411 \pm 0.0248, \rho = 0.2203\)), while raw Ridge regression fails completely (\(R^2 = -0.1810\)). Biologically, tissue loss in the cortex and hippocampus does not directly cause a patient to struggle with daily errands; instead, brain atrophy first erodes specific mental abilities (memory recall, executive attention), and it is that loss of mental ability that impairs daily functioning.
Modeling the Two-Step Pathway Multiplies Accuracy Over 6-Fold (\(R^2 \approx 0.265\)): When our 4-view models align structural brain MRI with the cognitive test battery along the natural pathway (\(\text{Brain MRI} \to \text{Cognition} \to \text{CDR-SB}\)), out-of-sample accuracy jumps more than six-fold:

LEND-SiMR + MAI [Mediated]: \(R^2 = 0.2648 \pm 0.0332\) (\(6.44\times\) higher than direct MRI, \(p = 9.77 \times 10^{-4}\))
SiMLR [Mediated]: \(R^2 = 0.2443 \pm 0.0534\) (\(5.94\times\) higher, solved in \(0.86\text{s}\))
Flow-SiMR-V + MAI [Mediated]: \(R^2 = 0.2290 \pm 0.0696\) (\(5.57\times\) higher) Formal Baron–Kenny mediation confirms that 84.5% to 86.4% of the total effect of brain atrophy on CDR-SB is indirect, traveling through cognitive performance (\(p < 10^{-15}\)).

Unconstrained Deep Networks Collapse on High-Dimensional Brain Data: Even with all four views available, unconstrained deep autoencoders fail (NED-SiMR + MAI: \(R^2 = 0.1127 \pm 0.0578\); NED-Shared-Private: \(R^2 = 0.0840\)). Without the orthogonal first-layer Stiefel constraint (\(\mathbf{V}_m^\top \mathbf{V}_m = \mathbf{I}\)), multi-layer perceptrons overfit noise across the 382 anatomical features and miss the shared brain-to-cognition axis.

title: 4  Discussion
section: 4.5 Normalizing Flows: Invertibility and Geodesic Trajectories
text:
4.5 Normalizing Flows: Invertibility and Geodesic Trajectories
The performance of Flow-SiMR-V arises from combining linear Stiefel filtering with bijective affine coupling layers:

Information Preservation: Unlike standard autoencoders that compress data through lossy bottlenecks with positive reconstruction error (\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}} > 0\)), normalizing flows are strictly bijective with unit or triangular Jacobian determinants (Dinh et al. 2016; Rezende and Mohamed 2015). Forward and inverse mappings are analytically exact.
Prior Regularization: Normalizing flows maximize exact log-likelihood under a standard multivariate Gaussian prior \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})\), acting as a continuous density regularizer that prevents coordinate collapse.
Stiefel Dimensionality Reduction: Prepending the linear projection \(\mathbf{V}_m\) compresses ambient observations to the intrinsic \(k\)-dimensional latent subspace before coupling layers operate. This reduces parameter counts and prevents flows from fitting high-frequency isotropic noise.


4.5.1 Geodesic Latent Trajectories
Because normalizing flows define a smooth diffeomorphism between the input subspace and the Gaussian latent space, Flow-SiMR-V enables continuous geodesic path interpolation. For a patient presenting with high disease risk at coordinate \(\mathbf{z}_{\text{start}}\), the linear trajectory toward a healthy reference \(\mathbf{z}_{\text{target}}\): \[
\mathbf{z}(t) = (1 - t) \mathbf{z}_{\text{start}} + t \mathbf{z}_{\text{target}}, \quad t \in [0, 1]
\] can be inverted through the flow and projected into observable feature space: \[
\mathbf{x}_m(t) = \text{Flow}_{\psi_m}^{-1}(\mathbf{z}(t)) \mathbf{V}_m^\top
\] This traces a continuous, physically grounded trajectory of biomarker changes across disease stages.

title: 4  Discussion
section: 4.6 Clinical Translation Across Cohorts and Translational Pathology
text:
4.6 Clinical Translation Across Cohorts and Translational Pathology
The modular Deep SiMLR framework addresses distinct clinical and biological challenges across the real-world clinical cohorts, neurodegenerative registries, neurotrauma models, and translational oncology:

Cleveland Heart Disease (Cardiovascular Diagnostic Profiling): Integrating resting clinical vitals (\(p_1 = 7\)) and stress electrocardiography/laboratory measures (\(p_2 = 6\)) across \(N = 297\) patients for binary coronary artery disease diagnosis (\(83.7\%\) test accuracy for NSAFlow-PCA and PCA, \(84.8\%\) linear probe). The OLEE matrix \(\mathbf{V}\) directly identifies exercise-induced ST depression (oldpeak), maximum heart rate (thalach), and chest pain type (cp) as the dominant orthogonal axes.
Diabetes Progression (Endocrine Risk Trajectories): Modeling quantitative 1-year disease progression from anthropometric baselines (\(p_1 = 5\)) and serum lipid biomarkers (\(p_2 = 5\)) across \(N = 442\) patients. The linear entrypoint attributes progression directly to body mass index (BMI) and serum triglycerides (S5), with NSAFlow-PCA (\(R^2 = 0.382\)) and SiMLR-LBFGSB (linear probe \(R^2 = 0.396\)) outperforming dense PCA (\(0.350\)).
Multiple Features (mfeat, High-Cardinality Multi-View Benchmarking): Integrating 4 core geometric/transform views (\(p = [76, 64, 6, 47]\)) in the initialization benchmark and all 6 views (\(p = [76, 216, 64, 240, 47, 6]\)) in the full mfeat6 benchmark across \(N = 2000\) samples, establishing that OLEE-constrained architectures effectively discover common consensus without view-dominance collapse.
ADNI Cognitive Mediation (Neurodegenerative Progression): As demonstrated in the 4-view ADNI-MCI cohort (\(N = 1,084\)), the OLEE contract enables the two-step brain-to-cognition-to-function pathway that unlocks a >6-fold accuracy gain (\(R^2 \approx 0.265\)) while insulating the model from the representation collapse observed in unconstrained deep networks.
Parkinson’s Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI): In longitudinal Parkinson’s disease cohorts (Marek et al. 2011), clinical trials require monitoring early dopaminergic denervation using \(^{123}\text{I}\)-ioflupane SPECT (DaTscan) striatal binding ratios, CSF \(\alpha\)-synuclein seed amplification assays, and motor UPDRS-III examinations. The OLEE contract ensures that striatal binding ratios maintain direct linear attribution, enabling auditable tracking of disease modification without black-box confounding.
Blast Neurotrauma and Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI): Low-level blast shockwave exposure induces diffuse axonal injury (DAI) characterized by non-local shear strains across white matter tracts (Stone et al. 2024). In these high-dimensional diffusion tensor imaging regimes, standard correlation objectives capitalize on chance associations. NSAFlow-PCA and SiMLR-LBFGSB enforce disjoint, non-negative support (\(\mathbf{V}^+ \odot \mathbf{V}^- = \mathbf{0}\)), isolating distinct anatomical tract disruptions without destructive crosstalk cancellation.
Translational Oncology (TCGA-BRCA & TCGA-KIRC): Across \(N = 822\) primary breast invasive carcinoma tumors in the primary benchmark (rna \(p_1=200\), cnv \(p_2=150\), rppa \(p_3=150\)) and \(N = 1,010\) tumors in the full-cohort audit (The Cancer Genome Atlas Network 2012; Cancer Discovery 2016), NSAFlow-PCA (\(92.7\%\)) and SiMLR-LBFGSB (\(93.0\%\) linear probe) isolate coordinated copy-number alterations, transcriptomic drivers (ESR1, GATA3, PGR), and targeted proteomics while preserving exact feature weights. In clear cell renal cell carcinoma (KIRC) (The Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network 2013), multi-omics integration aligns chromosomal 3p loss with downstream VHL-HIF1A angiogenic pathway activation.

title: 4  Discussion
text:
4.7 Methodological Considerations in Biomedical Cohorts
Our findings highlight three methodological principles for multi-modal analysis in computational anatomy and clinical cohorts:

Preprocessing Sensitivity (Centering vs. Standardization): In clinical neuroimaging (e.g., ADNI cortical thickness in millimeters), features share a common physical unit. Standardizing columns to unit variance (\(z\)-scoring) scales low-variance noise regions equally with high-variance atrophy hubs, which can alter or reverse downstream findings. When physical units are commensurate, mean-centering alone preserves genuine biological variance gradients.
Subspace Recovery vs. Axis Localization: An orthogonal rotation \(\mathbf{M} \in O(k)\) alters the orientation of basis axes without changing the linear subspace (\(\text{span}(\mathbf{X} \mathbf{V} \mathbf{M}) = \text{span}(\mathbf{X} \mathbf{V})\)). While linear prediction depends only on the subspace, localized biomarker discovery requires aligned, sparse, and non-negative axes—as demonstrated by the gap between PCA (\(\text{Support } F_1 = 0.333\)) and SiMLR-LBFGSB (\(\text{Support } F_1 = 0.942\)) on NonnegPartsWeak.
Dataset-Level Block Inference: Ranking multi-modal architectures must aggregate across replicate seeds within each dataset block before computing Friedman and Nemenyi statistics (Demšar 2006), avoiding artificial inflation of sample size from repeated random initializations.

title: 4  Discussion
text:
4.8 Limitations

First-Layer Linear Constraint: Restricting the input layer to an orthogonal Stiefel projection limits the model’s ability to capture high-order intra-modality non-linear feature interactions directly from raw inputs. When predictive signal is driven entirely by non-linear combinations within a single view, unconstrained deep encoders may achieve higher intra-modality expressivity.
Latent Dimension Scaling: Exact Stiefel retractions and polar factorizations scale cubically with latent rank (\(\mathcal{O}(k^3)\)). While efficient for typical biomedical latent spaces (\(k \le 64\)), scaling to massive latent spaces (\(k > 500\)) requires block-Stiefel or stochastic retraction methods.
Number of Benchmark Regimes: Block-level Nemenyi inference across \(B = 9\) datasets and \(k = 9\) models yields a conservative critical difference (\(CD = 4.004\)), requiring paired Wilcoxon and exact sign-flip permutation tests across the 27 paired runs to resolve finer pairwise differences.

title: 4  Discussion
text:
4.9 Conclusion
Deep SiMLR establishes a modular framework for multi-modal representation learning governed by the Only Linear Encoder Entrypoint (OLEE) contract. By decoupling linear feature attribution from downstream non-linear coordinate modeling, the architecture eliminates the clinical transparency penalty (\(\nabla_{\mathbf{X}_m} \mathbf{Z}_m = \mathbf{V}_m\)) and enables closed-form counterfactual recourse (\(\delta \mathbf{x}_m^* = \Delta \mathbf{z}_m^* \mathbf{V}_m^\top\)) while capturing complex manifold structure.
Across 243 benchmark evaluations spanning 3 real clinical/genomic cohorts and 6 synthetic manifolds, box-constrained Riemannian optimization (SiMLR-LBFGSB, rank \(3.28\), support \(F_1 = 0.942\)) and linear-encoder/non-linear-decoder hybrids (LEND, rank \(3.56\), predictive \(0.830\), \(CMC = 0.907\)) lead overall performance, while NSAFlow-PCA (rank \(3.61\), \(0.029\text{s}\)) matches dense PCA in speed while enforcing \(22.4\%\) disjoint sparsity with zero crosstalk. Every OLEE-constrained architecture significantly outperforms unconstrained deep autoencoders (NED, NEDPP, \(p_{\text{Holm}} \le 0.018\)). In longitudinal neurodegeneration (ADNI-MCI, \(N=1,084\)), the OLEE contract unlocks a >6-fold cognitive mediation gain on clinical dementia severity (\(R^2 \approx 0.2648, p < 10^{-15}\)) while preventing the overfitting collapse that afflicts unconstrained deep networks.

A.1 Multi-Omic Integration Strategy
We evaluated the Only Linear Encoder Entrypoint (OLEE) across all nine benchmark architectures using the three-view TCGA-BRCA breast invasive carcinoma cohort (\(N = 822\) primary tumors with complete multi-omic profiles and adjudicated clinical receptor status, cached at data/tcga/brca_er_cached.npz) (The Cancer Genome Atlas Network 2012; Cancer Discovery 2016). The dataset integrates three distinct molecular assay platforms:
The downstream clinical target is binary Estrogen Receptor (ER) status (Positive vs. Negative, \(76.4\%\) ER+ prevalence), evaluated across \(N_{\text{seeds}} = 3\) independent \(70/30\) stratified train/test splits (Seeds 42, 43, 44, standardized strictly inside the training fold, with consolidate = False and default "pca" initialization).

title: Appendix A — Multi-omics Clinical Validation (TCGA-BRCA)

title: Appendix B — Operational Implementation and Complexity
text:
B.1.1 Training Algorithm
Initialize {V_m, theta_m, phi_m}
For epoch t in 1..T:
    1. Calculate alpha_t (Stiefel mixing coefficient)
       - alpha_t = min(1.0, t / (Total_Epochs * ramp_ratio))
    2. Forward Pass:
       # Apply OLEE
       V_active = (1 - alpha_t) * V_raw + alpha_t * NewtonSchulz(V_raw)
       Z_m = Encoder(X_m, V_active, theta_m)
       
       # For NEDPP: Disentangle Shared vs Private
       U_shared, P_private = Split(Z_m)
       Loss_disentangle = CovariancePenalty(U_shared, P_private)
       
    3. Consensus Estimation:
       - U_hat = Average(Z_1, ..., Z_M) or NewtonSchulzConsensus(Z_list)
    4. Calculate Total Energy J:
       - J = (1 - alpha_t) * L_recon + alpha_t * L_align + gamma * L_disentangle
    5. Backpropagate gradients to {V_raw, theta_m, phi_m}
    6. Update weights via Optimizer (Adam with weight decay)

B.2 Mathematical Derivations

B.2.1 Riemannian Updates
We implement Riemannian updates on the Stiefel manifold via projection onto the tangent space \(\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{V}} \mathbb{V}_{k,n}\). We compute the Riemannian gradient \(\text{grad} \mathcal{J}(\mathbf{V})\) from the Euclidean gradient \(\nabla \mathcal{J}(\mathbf{V})\): \[ \text{grad} \mathcal{J}(\mathbf{V}) = \nabla \mathcal{J}(\mathbf{V}) - \mathbf{V} \text{sym}(\mathbf{V}^\top \nabla \mathcal{J}(\mathbf{V})) \]
The orthogonal penalty \(\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{V}) = \frac{1}{4} \| \mathbf{V}^\top \mathbf{V} - \mathbf{I}_k \|_F^2\) permits a Taylor expansion for a perturbation \(\Delta\): \[ \mathcal{P}(\mathbf{V} + \Delta) \approx \frac{1}{4} \text{Tr}\left( (\mathbf{V}^\top \Delta + \Delta^\top \mathbf{V})^2 \right) \] This penalty evaluates to zero for any \(\Delta\) strictly within the tangent space.


B.2.2 Newton-Schulz Convergence
We enforce orthogonality via the iteration sequence: \[ \mathbf{Y}_{k+1} = \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{Y}_k (3\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{Y}_k^\top \mathbf{Y}_k) \] The residual error \(\mathbf{E}_k = \mathbf{I} - \mathbf{Y}_k^\top \mathbf{Y}_k\) obeys the relation \(\mathbf{E}_{k+1} = \frac{3}{4} \mathbf{E}_k^2 + \frac{1}{4} \mathbf{E}_k^3\). This yields quadratic convergence: \(\| \mathbf{E}_{k+1} \|_2 < \| \mathbf{E}_k \|_2^2\).


B.2.3 Noise Reduction Law
Assuming independent noise distributions \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_m \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \sigma^2 \mathbf{I})\), the consensus variance scales as: \[ \text{Var}\left( \frac{1}{M} \sum_{m=1}^M \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_m \right) = \frac{\sigma^2}{M} \] The corresponding \(100(1-\delta)\%\) confidence interval for the underlying signal \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) is bounded by: \[ \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\text{consensus}} \pm z_{\delta/2} \sqrt{\frac{\sigma^2}{M}(1-\rho) + \rho\sigma^2} \] The covariance term \(\rho\sigma^2\) provides the strict statistical lower bound for the multi-modal consensus error.

B.3.1 Modality Weights (\(w\))
We bound the Statistical Influence Function \(\mathcal{I}_m = \frac{\partial \mathbf{U}}{\partial w_m}\) by the spectral gap \((\lambda_1 - \lambda_2)^{-1}\) of the input feature covariance \(\Sigma_m\). Consequently, SiMLR operational sensitivity scales proportionally with the degree of multicollinearity in the input domain.


B.3.2 \(\alpha\)-Transition
The mixing parameter \(\alpha\) controls the trade-off between independent modality reconstruction and cross-modal consensus alignment. We set the transition point at the epoch where the first derivative of the consensus variance approaches zero.

text:
B.9 Technical Glossary

Normalizing Flow: A family of deep generative models that transforms a simple probability distribution (e.g., standard multivariate Gaussian) into a complex distribution using a sequence of invertible, bijective mappings via the change-of-variables theorem.
Bijective Mapping: A mathematically exact, one-to-one and onto function. In Flow-SiMR, bijectivity guarantees that the forward mapping (encoding) and inverse mapping (decoding) preserve information perfectly with zero reconstruction error (\(\mathcal{L}_{MSE} = 0\)).
Affine Coupling Layer: The core building block of RealNVP normalizing flows. It splits the input features into two halves, copying one partition directly while scaling and translating the other half using arbitrary non-linear neural networks (which do not need to be invertible themselves).
OLEE (Only Linear Encoder Entry-point): An architectural constraint that restricts the entry layer of a deep neural network to be an orthogonal linear projection. This forms a structural information bottleneck that prevents deep layers from memorizing noise.
NSA-Flow (Non-negative Stiefel Approximating Flow): A smooth, fully differentiable optimization penalty used to constrain the linear encoder basis matrix \(\mathbf{V}_m\) to the Stiefel manifold (\(\mathbf{V}_m^\top \mathbf{V}_m = \mathbf{I}_K\)) during backpropagation, replacing hard SVD projections.
Schur Complement: A matrix operation used to compute the conditional mean and covariance of a partitioned multivariate Gaussian distribution in closed form, enabling mathematically valid cross-view imputation.
Leave-One-Out (LOO) Topology: An optimization pathway where each view’s latent representation is aligned against a consensus target computed exclusively from all other views, preventing the model from learning trivial identity mappings.
Modality Alignment Index (MAI): A metric (typically based on Procrustes \(R^2\)) that quantifies the alignment fidelity between an individual view’s latent space and the global consensus.
Spectral Sharpness: A random-matrix-theory-based metric evaluating singular value concentrations to identify and suppress isotropic high-dimensional noise, preventing it from corrupting the consensus representation.
Classical SiMLR: Similarity-driven Multi-view Linear Reconstruction. Strictly linear baseline architecture assuming Euclidean projection of modalities.
LEND: Linear Encoder, Deep Decoder. Combines OLEE-constrained linear encoder with a deep non-linear decoder, balancing interpretability and reconstruction fidelity.
NED: Non-linear Encoder-Decoder. Applies non-linear MLP transformations to both encoder (post-OLEE) and decoder, maximizing representational capacity.
NEDPP: Non-linear Encoder-Decoder with Private Partitions. Disentangles modality-specific private variance from shared cross-modal consensus.
Flow-SiMR: Normalizing Flow Similarity-driven Multi-view Representation. Integrates bijective normalizing flows with latent consensus alignment for information-preserving multi-modal integration.
Flow-SiMR-V: Flow-SiMR with a linear projection matrix (OLEE) entry point to allow feature attribution while maintaining deep flow-based mappings.

C.1 Model Formulation
To resolve the “Information Masking” problem inherent in deep multi-modal normalizing flows, we introduce Flow-SiMR-V, which pre-pends a Stiefel-constrained linear encoder matrix \(\mathbf{V}_m\) to each view’s Normalizing Flow. This architecture establishes a strict globally interpretable information bottleneck at the input entry point while retaining bijective density mapping and conditional inference on the consensus latent space. The underlying normalizing flows are implemented natively in PyTorch, adapting structures from the Latent-Aligned Multiview Normalizing Flows (LAMNr Flows) open-source framework (ntustison/LAMNrFlows).

C.1.1 Mathematical Formulation
For each input modality \(\mathbf{X}_m \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D_m}\):

Only Linear Encoder Entry (OLEE) Bottleneck: \[\mathbf{Z}_m = \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m, \quad \text{subject to } \mathbf{V}_m^\top \mathbf{V}_m = \mathbf{I}_K\] where \(\mathbf{V}_m \in \mathbb{R}^{D_m \times K}\) is regularized via Non-negative Stiefel Approximating Flow (NSA-Flow) and sparsity quantile thresholding.
Low-Dimensional Bijective Normalizing Flow: \[\mathbf{U}_m = f_{\text{flow}, m}(\mathbf{Z}_m)\] where \(f_{\text{flow}, m}: \mathbb{R}^K \to \mathbb{R}^K\) is a bijective transform mapping the projected coordinate to the shared latent coordinate.
Consensus and Inverse Reconstruction: \[\mathbf{U}_{\text{consensus}} = \text{mixing}(\mathbf{U}_1, \dots, \mathbf{U}_M)\] \[\mathbf{X}_m^{\text{recon}} = f_{\text{flow}, m}^{-1}(\mathbf{U}_{\text{consensus}}) \mathbf{V}_m^\top\]

text:
C.3 Algorithm for Flow-SiMR-V with Delayed Gating Warmup
To stably optimize the joint-variational objective under dynamic modality weighting without triggering weight collapse, we train the linear encoders, normalizing flows, and dynamic weights using the Block-Coordinate Descent (BCD) procedure detailed below.

C.3.1 Algorithmic Flow
For a set of \(M\) data matrices \(\mathbf{X}_1, \dots, \mathbf{X}_M\), shared latent rank \(K\), and max training epochs \(E\):

Forward Pass:

Project features to low-dimensional space: \(\mathbf{Z}_m = \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m\) for \(m=1, \dots, M\).
Apply normalizing flows: \(\mathbf{U}_m = f_{\text{flow}, m}(\mathbf{Z}_m)\) and extract shared consensus latents \(\mathbf{Z}_{m, \text{shared}} = \mathbf{U}_{m, 1:K}\).
Compute shared consensus coordinates using Newton-Schulz or ICA mixing: \(\mathbf{U}_{\text{consensus}} = \text{mixing}(\mathbf{Z}_{1, \text{shared}}, \dots, \mathbf{Z}_{M, \text{shared}})\).

Delayed Gating (Modality Gating Schedule):

For epoch \(t < T_{\text{delayed}}\): set modality weights uniformly \(w_m = 1/M\).
For epoch \(t \ge T_{\text{delayed}}\):

Compute the Leave-One-Out (LOO) consensus target for each view: \(\mathbf{U}_{\neq m} = \sum_{j \neq m} w_j \mathbf{Z}_{j, \text{shared}}\).
Compute the Modality Alignment Index: \(\text{MAI}_m = 1 - \frac{\|\mathbf{Z}_{m, \text{shared}}\Omega - \mathbf{U}_{\neq m}\|_F^2}{\|\mathbf{U}_{\neq m}\|_F^2}\).
Update gating weights: \(w_m = (1 - \rho) \cdot \frac{1}{M} + \rho \cdot \text{softmax}(\tau \cdot \text{MAI}_m)\) (with exponential ramp-up \(\rho\)).


Loss Computation & Backpropagation:

Compute reconstruction loss: \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}} = \sum_m \|\mathbf{X}_m - \hat{\mathbf{X}}_m\|_F^2\) where \(\hat{\mathbf{X}}_m = f_{\text{flow}, m}^{-1}([\mathbf{U}_{\text{consensus}} \parallel \mathbf{0}])\mathbf{V}_m^\top\).
Compute alignment loss: \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{align}} = \sum_m \|\mathbf{Z}_{m, \text{shared}}\Omega - \mathbf{U}_{\neq m}\|_F^2\).
Backpropagate gradients to update linear projections \(\mathbf{V}_m\) and flow parameters.
Retract \(\mathbf{V}_m\) onto the Stiefel manifold using NSA-Flow Newton-Schulz updates.

D.3.1 Block-Level Sign-Flip Permutation Floor
In statistical hypothesis testing between paired models across \(B = 9\) independent dataset blocks (where each block cell is the mean across \(N_{\text{seeds}} = 3\) replicates, following Demšar (2006)), the exact distribution-free sign-flip null distribution across the \(B = 9\) blocks consists of \(2^B = 512\) equally probable sign assignments: \[
p_{\text{perm}} = \frac{1}{2^B} \sum_{\mathbf{s} \in \{-1, +1\}^B} \mathbb{I}\left(\left|\frac{1}{B} \sum_{i=1}^B s_i \Delta_i\right| \ge |\bar{\Delta}|\right)
\]
For \(B = 9\) independent dataset blocks (or \(N = 10\) independent seeds in the ADNI-MCI 4-view mediation benchmark), the minimal attainable two-sided permutation \(p\)-value occurs when every block favours the same model: \[
p_{\min, B=9} = \frac{2}{2^9} = \frac{2}{512} \approx 0.003906, \qquad p_{\min, N=10} = \frac{2}{2^{10}} = \frac{2}{1024} \approx 0.001953
\]
We enforce the following statistical standards throughout the manuscript:

Zero Unadjusted Pooled \(p\)-values: We completely eliminate pooled repeated-measures \(t\)-tests and unaggregated seed-rows in global Friedman/Wilcoxon tests (build_ranking_blocks). Crossing multiple seeds or hyperparameters on the same dataset does not increase dataset-level degrees of freedom.
Floor Truncation: No distribution-free permutation test can report a value below \(2/2^B\).
Triple Metric Reporting: Global consensus prediction (\(Y\) on \(\mathbf{U}\)), strictly linear first-layer accuracy (\(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}\)), and axis-sensitive random forest probe accuracy on \(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}\) are reported alongside ground-truth latent (\(CMC\)) and sparse support Jaccard recovery.

D.5 Determinism and RNG Isolation
To ensure absolute determinism across all benchmark runs:

Process RNG Isolation: Invocations of normalizing flow retractions and torch optimization loops restore CPU and CUDA generator states upon completion. No model fitting operation mutates the caller’s global random state.
Fixed Random Seeds: The primary deep ranking benchmark iterates over seeds \(42, 43, 44\) (\(N_{\text{seeds}} = 3\), with --seeds 10 configurable for extended runs up to seed \(51\)), while the ADNI-MCI 4-view mediation benchmark evaluates across 10 seeds (\(42, \dots, 51\)). Data synthesis, train/test splitting (\(70/30\)), and neural network parameter initialization are strictly controlled by these seed parameters.
